pg006_n0005: This textbook, Fine Art for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0006: It is written in accordance with the twenty twenty-three Fine Art Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form One to Form Four, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, MoEST.
pg006_n0007: It is a revised edition of Fine Art for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form One that was published in twenty twenty-three in accordance with the two thousand and five syllabus issued by the then Ministry of Education and Vocational Training, M O E V T.
pg006_n0009: The book consists of six chapters, namely; Introduction to Fine Art, Fundamentals of Drawing, Fundamentals to Painting, Fundamentals of Printmaking, Trends of Fine Art in Tanzania, and Occupational Health and Environmental Care.
pg006_n0010: Each chapter contains text, activities, scenarios, illustrations, and exercises.
pg006_n0011: You are encouraged to do all the activities and exercises as well as other assignments provided by your teacher.
pg006_n0012: You are also required to prepare a portfolio for keeping records for activities performed in different lessons.
pg006_n0013: Doing so will enable you to develop the intended competencies.
pg006_n0015: Additional learning resources are available at the T I E e-library: o l dot tie dot go dot t z, or o l dot tie dot go dot t z.

pg007_n0009: Fine art plays a great role in our daily activities and touches every aspect of our lives in many ways.
pg007_n0010: The images you see in various books, the emblem printed on your uniform, and the decorations you perceive at various places are some examples of fine art products.
pg007_n0011: It is also an important aspect of our culture.
pg007_n0012: Different societies in the world have been making and using fine art products for different purposes.
pg007_n0013: These include storytelling, ceremonial occasion and prestige.
pg007_n0014: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of fine art, its principles, elements of fine art, and its relationships with other disciplines.
pg007_n0015: The competencies developed will enable you to appreciate fine art and later on become an entrepreneur in creating and selling artwork.

pg007_n0022: To better understand the concept of fine art, let us have the general meaning of art and its various forms.
pg007_n0024: Art refers to the general term comprising human creativity and imagination to produce various art forms.
pg007_n0025: For many years, people have been using different art forms to express feelings, ideas, emotions and thoughts.
pg007_n0026: Additionally, art has been regarded as the highest form of expression in human life.
pg007_n0027: Through various art forms, artists create works of art that are used as an alternative communication to deliver the desired messages.
pg007_n0028: A form of art is made of all external or physical characteristics of an artwork.
pg007_n0029: It also depends on the size and type of materials or media used in the creation of a work of art.
pg007_n0030: Artists use different art forms to express their imagination and give tangible or visual structures to their creative ideas.
pg008_n0006: There are three main forms of art namely visual, literary, and performing arts.
pg008_n0007: These forms are explained as follows:
pg008_n0011: These are creative works of art that are appreciated or enjoyed by eyesight.
pg008_n0012: Examples of visual arts are drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, design, craftworks, photography, filmmaking and architecture.
pg008_n0013: These works of art are created to express the artist’s ideas and imagination in visual forms.
pg008_n0014: Visual arts are among the major tools for teaching and learning in many ways.
pg008_n0015: They include the use of illustration in books, digital presentations and other teaching aids such as spheres, toys, periodicals and photographs.
pg008_n0016: Applying visual arts skills and knowledge makes learning enjoyable because it helps students relate classroom activities to outdoor activities such as domestic chores.
pg008_n0020: The term literary arts refer to a form of art which is delivered in a spoken or written form.
pg008_n0021: Literary arts include poems, plays, stories, novels as well as other creative works which are closely related to spoken or written communication.
pg008_n0022: Works of literary art include magazines, letters, manuscripts, and books.
pg008_n0023: Literary arts have different genres such as drama, poetry, and prose.
pg008_n0024: Each genre distinguishes itself in the essence of how it presents messages.
pg008_n0028: Performing arts is a form of art in which a range of artistic activities are presented on the stage before an audience.
pg008_n0029: These kinds of arts include acrobatics, music and theatre which are performed through body balance, vocals and instruments as well as life experiences respectively.
pg008_n0033: Fine art refers to forms of visual arts that are primarily produced and valued for their aesthetic, utilitarian and intellectual significance.
pg008_n0034: The origin of fine art is human activities involved in creative processes.
pg008_n0035: These processes involve preparations, incubation or putting together production ideas and materials, composition of a work of art, evaluation of the work of art, and production or completion of a work of art.
pg009_n0003: Fine artists use their creativity, skills and personal perceptions to communicate their own or other people’s emotions, ideas, and observations about the world.
pg009_n0004: Fine art is a potential means of expression for artists to comment on personal, cultural, social and political issues.
pg009_n0006: Fine artworks can be found in various places including residential areas, art shops, galleries, public spaces, museums, individual collections and online sources, for example, art finder dot com.
pg009_n0010: Fine arts cover a wide range of artistic skills that are created and appreciated for their beauty and expressive power.
pg009_n0011: With the advancement of technology, artists are exposed to various techniques and media to create tangible and visual ideas.
pg009_n0012: This development extends several fine art forms which include drawing, painting, design, printmaking and sculpture.
pg009_n0013: These forms are further explained as follows:
pg009_n0017: This is a process of creating images on a surface using a marking tool such as a pencil, charcoal or crayon.
pg009_n0018: Drawing is a basic step when developing other forms of fine art including painting and designing.
pg009_n0019: A drawing can also be used as an independent work of art to portray a message to an audience.

pg010_n0004: This is a form of fine art in which ideas, thoughts, emotions, and feelings are creatively expressed by using coloured images.
pg010_n0005: Painting is a work of art made from paints.
pg010_n0006: Painting can be made on walls, paper and canvas by using brushes and colours.
pg010_n0007: A good choice and effective application of colours in painting create a skilful and complete composition.
pg010_n0008: In addition, the skilful use of colours adds aesthetic value to paintings in particular and the general surroundings in which they are displayed.

pg010_n0015: This is a three-dimensional art form that involves the creation of physical objects or forms by manipulating and shaping materials.
pg010_n0016: Sculptures can be produced by using a variety of media or materials.
pg010_n0017: These include clay, wax, wood, paper, stone, metal, fabric, rubber, glass, gypsum powder and cement.
pg010_n0018: Sculpture can be figurative or non-figurative work of art.
pg010_n0019: A complete sculpture can be in relief; showing three dimensions of the artwork, in intaglio and free-standing or sculpture in the round.
pg010_n0020: Examples of sculpture works include a bust, a statue and a figurine.

pg011_n0009: Design is another form of art.
pg011_n0010: It is defined as an outline, a sketch, or a visual idea of a work of art to be created.
pg011_n0011: Works of art such as textile designs, posters, emblems, logos and banners are known as products of design.
pg011_n0012: This is because they appear as mere sketches or outlines throughout the process of creation; until they are produced as complete works of art.
pg011_n0013: Design also refers to the creative activity of planning and organising elements of art, such as lines, shapes, colours, textures and space, in a work of art.

pg013_n0012: Functions of fine art in human life
pg013_n0014: Throughout the history of human civilisation, people have been using different forms of art as means to communicate various ideas and express their feelings.
pg013_n0015: Similarly, Fine art plays different important roles in our life.
pg013_n0016: These include educational, historical and identity preservation, economic, political, social, religious, and cultural roles.
pg013_n0017: It is also source of enjoyment in our life.
pg013_n0018: These functions can be elaborated as follows:
pg013_n0022: Fine art has the power to improve understanding and change people’s behaviour through the incorporation of educational themes into works of art.
pg013_n0023: The art can be used in different contexts, such as making teaching aids like, book illustrations, map, and caricature drawing.
pg013_n0024: It is also used in campaigning materials like posters and banners, because it fosters understanding and creativity; improves the ability to analyse; and provides a platform for self-expression.
pg013_n0028: Drawing, painting, printmaking, and sculpture, frequently contain images reflecting the history, culture, and identity of a particular society.
pg013_n0029: They are passed down to new generations through art, which helps maintain a sense of oneness and belonging among members of a particular cultural group.
pg013_n0033: Artists earn income by selling artworks or exhibiting on different platforms such as in local art galleries, museums and online markets.
pg013_n0034: They may also be commissioned to produce artwork for various events.
pg013_n0035: The earned income helps them boost individual economies, improve life standards as well as contribute to the national income through taxes and other forms of payment.
pg014_n0004: artists earn income from their artworks, they have to protect their work through copyrights.
pg014_n0005: This is very important because if they do not do so their work can be reproduced or duplicated and make pirates benefit from it.
pg014_n0006: Copyright is a type of intellectual property that protects original works of authorship as soon as an author fixes the work in a tangible form of expression.
pg014_n0007: Tanzania’s Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act of nineteen ninety-nine makes it illegal for anyone to use protected work without the author’s permission during the author’s lifetime plus fifty years.
pg014_n0008: In Tanzania, copyright issues are taken care by the Copyright Society of Tanzania, COSOTA.
pg014_n0012: Some forms of art are used to raise awareness on political issues.
pg014_n0013: They also promote democracy and liberation.
pg014_n0014: Banners, posters and monuments for political leaders are good examples of how fine art is used in politics.
pg014_n0015: In performing art; music, poetry, and drama serve the purpose of delivering the intended messages such as encouraging positive changes and development as well as promoting peace based on the current political situations.
pg014_n0019: Is concerned with social life of different people.
pg014_n0020: It expresses ideas and emotions in different ways.
pg014_n0021: For example, in various societies, art is a means of transferring knowledge, transmitting customs, morals and religious values and advocating good manners and proper social values to both elders and the young.
pg014_n0022: Moreover, art has been used in many societies to express emotions and appreciation.
pg014_n0026: Artworks can be used to influence cultural and traditional values, promote self-esteem, entertain, warn and educate people on morals and customs.
pg014_n0027: Moreover, artworks can be used to inspire socio-economic changes through activities such as art exhibition, traditional dances and festivals, worshipping ceremonies, drama, paintings and songs.
pg014_n0028: To a great extent, these works of art are important for enhancing cultural development.
pg014_n0032: When someone looks at a beautiful artwork, it might be enjoyable for them.
pg014_n0033: Art enhances aesthetic satisfaction and enlivens our lives with beauty and creativity by stimulating our senses, evoking emotions, and presenting us with new perspectives.

pg015_n0022: Fine art manifestation is an expression that describes how art can be seen from nature.
pg015_n0023: Fine art manifests itself from two sources which are nature and human activities.
pg015_n0024: Fine art manifestations from nature can be observed in our surrounding environment and through all living organisms such as plants, insects, animals, and human beings.
pg015_n0025: This shows that art can freely manifest itself in nature independent from human activities.
pg015_n0026: Examples of fine art manifestation in nature can be seen in various environmental phenomena such as sunrise and sunset, rainbow and physical features such as landscapes.
pg015_n0027: Fine art manifestations in nature can be expressed in plants, insects and animals.
pg015_n0029: Fine art manifestation in plants: Fine art manifests itself in plants in different ways.
pg015_n0030: For instance, some plants are rich in colours; other plants have attractive fruits and leaves.
pg015_n0031: Examples of plants with colourful flowers include roses, perennial bulb plants and sunflower.
pg015_n0032: Plants like apple, mango and grape trees bear beautiful fruits.
pg015_n0033: Other plants display beauty through their leaves.
pg015_n0034: These include the coleus plant which has colourful leaves and aglaonema which has spotted leaves.

pg021_n0013: Principles of fine art are sometimes known as principles of design or principles of art.
pg021_n0014: These are guidelines used by artists in the art composition process.
pg021_n0015: When successfully applied, the principles guarantee accuracy in all actions and decisions taken in the making of the final work of art.
pg021_n0016: Principles of art are guidelines that help artists focus on the process of creating a pleasant work of art.
pg021_n0017: These principles include balance, proportion, emphasis, variety, rhythm, movement, harmony and unity.
pg021_n0018: The details for each are as follows:
pg021_n0022: The principle of balance is an equilibrium achieved through a good arrangement of visual elements such as line, texture, colour and form.
pg021_n0023: When balance is achieved in a work of art, it makes the work stable where it is placed.
pg021_n0024: In design, balance is categorised into three types, namely formal balance, informal balance and radial balance.
pg021_n0025: These types are explained as follows:
pg021_n0029: Formal balance is also called symmetrical balance which refers to an equilibrium achieved by arranging similar or identical elements on both sides of the axis.
pg021_n0030: An axis is an imaginary horizontal or vertical line assumed to be drawn at the centre of a design.
pg021_n0031: A formal balance has two sides of a composition with equal visual weight.
pg021_n0032: Figure one point fifteen shows an example of formal balance.
pg021_im001: Two examples of formal balance: a pair of scissors arranged along a horizontal axis and a fleur-de-lis arranged along a vertical axis, each divided by a dashed line showing symmetry.
pg021_n0036: Figure one point fifteen: Formal balance
pg022_n0006: Informal balance is also known as asymmetrical balance.
pg022_n0007: It is a process of arranging two unlike objects in a work of art to create equal visual weight.
pg022_n0008: Figure one point sixteen shows an example of informal balance.
pg022_im004: A line drawing of informal balance on a mantelpiece: a small dark bowl sits on the left, while a clock and a tall candlestick are grouped on the right to create equal visual weight with unlike objects.

pg022_n0015: Radial balance occurs when the elements of design seem to radiate out from the centre of a design.
pg022_n0016: A good example of radial balance can be seen on flower petals, tree rings, a half-cut orange and a bicycle wheel.
pg022_n0017: Figure one point seventeen shows the radial balance of motifs.
pg022_im001: A cross-section of an orange with wedges arranged evenly around the centre, showing radial balance as the pattern spreads outward in all directions.
pg022_n0019: Figure one point seventeen: The radial balance of motifs
pg023_n0006: The principle of proportion refers to size relationships between elements of art in a composition or work of art.
pg023_n0007: A well-proportioned work of art displays a relative scale between height, width and depth of elements of design.

pg027_n0025: These are sometimes known as elements of design or elements of art.
pg027_n0026: In fine art, communication is done through symbols or signs.

pg027_n0029: The visual elements of art are line, shape, form, space, value, colour and texture.
pg027_n0030: These elements are explained as follows:
pg027_n0034: This is a basic element of art which is defined as a moving point in space.
pg027_n0035: When two or more points are joined, a line is formed.
pg027_n0036: A line is a fundamental element of art because it is applied in the formation of other elements such as shapes, forms and texture.
pg027_n0037: The major types of lines are vertical lines, horizontal lines, diagonal lines, zigzag lines and curved lines.
pg027_n0040: These are straight lines moving up and down in a space without any slant.
pg027_n0041: They are used to suggest height and strength.

pg028_n0007: Horizontal lines: These are straight lines parallel to the horizon drawn from left to right.
pg028_n0008: They are used to suggest width, distance, calmness and stability.

pg028_im002: Several horizontal black lines of different lengths and thicknesses stacked one above another to show horizontal lines.
pg028_n0011: Figure one point two six: Horizontal lines
pg028_n0013: Diagonal lines: These are straight lines that slant in any direction except vertically or horizontally.
pg028_n0014: They are used to suggest a sense of movement and lack of stability.

pg029_n0005: They are used to suggest feelings of nervousness and confusion.

pg030_n0006: Lines can be either actual lines or implied lines as discussed below:
pg030_n0008: Actual lines: These are real linear marks made in a composition.
pg030_n0009: They are lines appearing as a solid connection between one or more points in space.
pg030_n0010: Actual lines vary in width, character and thickness qualities, depending on the medium used to draw the lines.
pg030_n0012: Implied lines: These are imaginary lines and are suggested by changes in colour, tone, texture or by the edge of shapes of objects and structures in the environment.
pg030_n0013: A good example of an implied line is the horizon line which separates the sky and the ground.
pg030_n0017: This is an element of art expressed by two dimensions with only length and width.
pg030_n0018: All shapes fall into only two categories which are geometrical and organic shapes.
pg030_n0020: Geometrical shapes: These are also known as regular shapes.
pg030_n0021: Geometrical shapes have specific names such as circle, triangle, square, rectangular and oval.

pg031_n0002: Figure one point three zero: Geometrical shapes

pg031_n0005: Generally, they have no proper names and are natural in their origin.

pg031_n0008: Figure one point three one: Organic shapes
pg031_n0012: This is an element of art made of mass or shape of a work of art.
pg031_n0013: Similarly, a form of a work of art or an object comprises its length, width and height.
pg031_n0014: An artist must have a good understanding of the concept of form to be flexible and competent in his creative activities.
pg031_n0015: Forms are categorised into two types which are geometrical or regular forms and organic or irregular forms.

pg032_n0012: They are also called free form because they are indefinite.
pg032_n0013: Examples of organic forms include stones, trees and potatoes.

pg032_n0020: This is an element of art that is created by an area around, above, below and within an object.
pg032_n0021: Space is significant in the creation of the illusion of depth in a painting or drawing.
pg032_n0022: Space in art is categorised into two types which are positive and negative space.
pg033_n0002: Positive space: This is a space occupied by the shape or form of an object.
pg033_n0003: Positive space is an area of interest or main focus in artwork.

pg033_n0009: It helps an artist break a composition into different parts to capture the subject matter with its appropriate proportion and balance.

pg034_n0018: This is the surface quality of an object or the way an object’s surface feels.
pg034_n0019: In fine art, texture refers to rough or smooth visual quality.
pg034_n0020: Texture in art is categorised into two.
pg034_n0021: These are tactile or actual texture and visual or simulated texture.
pg034_n0024: This is the real texture of an object which can be felt by physical contact.

pg052_n0008: It is very important to take good care of all drawing materials and equipment before, during and after class or studio activities.
pg052_n0009: This is because the value of a work of art relies on the quality of materials and the equipment used to create it.
pg052_n0010: Besides, art materials and equipment are fragile and very expensive.
pg052_n0011: It is advised to keep art materials and tools in a storage or studio where safety and quality of the equipment are properly observed.
pg052_n0012: The following is safety guidance on handling art materials and equipment:
pg052_n0016: Drawing materials and equipment should be stored in a safe place when they are not in use.
pg052_n0019: Drawing books should be kept away from any liquid materials to avoid wetting.
pg052_n0022: Flammable tools like rubber erasers, plastics, rulers, and oil colours that use turpentine should be kept away from any source of heat or fire.
pg052_n0025: Brushes should be cleaned well with proper solvents after each use.
pg052_n0028: Liquid materials such as fixative sprays, linseed oils, and solvents should not be left open to avoid contamination by dusting to prevent them from drying out due to air exposure.
pg052_n0031: Drawing papers should not be folded before and after use.
pg052_n0034: Do not use sharp tools such as a razor blade, or a knife for cutting anything on the drawing-board surface or table.
pg052_n0035: This includes cutting stencils and trimming papers.
pg052_n0036: More often, such acts distort the surface of a drawing board.
pg052_n0039: Clean erasers with clean-soft-cloth material after use and pack them into their package or container.
pg052_n0040: Doing so helps to keep erasers clean for the next user.
pg052_n0043: Do not use pins for fitting your paper on the drawing board, instead use artistic clips or artistic tape.
pg052_n0046: Drawing materials containing fluid, for example, fountain marker pens should be kept facing down or laid horizontally to avoid leakage.

pg054_n0015: Shading is one of the steps in drawing which involves many drawing techniques.
pg054_n0016: It is a process of drawing by adding tonal values to a drawn image to create an illusion of depth or a three-dimensional effect.
pg054_n0017: Shading is also important in drawing because it enhances form by creating an illusion of light in a drawing.

pg055_n0006: There are several shading techniques used in drawing.
pg055_n0007: Some of them include hatching, cross-hatching, smudging, dotting and scribbling.
pg055_n0011: This is a technique of shading by drawing parallel lines in the same direction.
pg055_n0012: When the lines are drawn closer together, they form darker values and when drawn with space between lines a lighter value is created.

pg056_n0006: Cross-hatching: This is a shading technique by drawing lines across each other.
pg056_n0008: When lines are drawn closer together, they form darker values.
pg056_n0009: Similarly, when lines are drawn leaving space, they make a lighter value.
pg056_n0010: Figure two point twenty-three shows cross-hatching shading technique.

pg056_n0015: This is a technique of shading made by smearing light or dark values on a drawing with a pencil or charcoal.
pg056_n0017: The smudging technique is also known as blending.

pg056_n0020: Figure two point twenty-four: smudging or blending shading technique
pg057_n0006: This is a technique of shading by using dots.
pg057_n0007: When dots are concentrated in the same area of a drawing, they form a darker value and evenly distributed dots form a lighter value.

pg057_n0014: This is a shading technique in a drawing which is applied by manipulating controlled and uncontrolled strokes of a drawing tool such as a pencil or charcoal to create a shade.
pg057_n0015: It is a common shading technique used by artists when drawing portraits and still-life drawings.

pg063_n0015: Role of a simple decorative drawing
pg063_n0017: From different perspectives, a simple decorative drawing plays a significant role in our daily life.
pg063_n0018: Some of them are outlined as follows:
pg063_n0020: Aesthetic appearance: It adds beauty and visual attraction to our surroundings.
pg063_n0021: It can transform ordinary spaces into inviting, attractive, and inspiring environments.
pg063_n0022: A well-decorated room, for example, can create a positive atmosphere and uplift the user’s mood.
pg063_n0024: Personal identity: It provides a means for individuals to express their personalities, interests, and preferences.
pg063_n0025: Whether it is through the choice of colours, patterns, artwork, or objects, decorations allow us to create things that reflect who we are and what we value.
pg063_n0027: Creating comfort: It can enhance the comfort of a space.
pg063_n0028: For example, cool colours and warm lighting can make a living room more inviting and a comfortable place to stay.
pg063_n0030: Setting the mood: It can influence our emotions and set the mood for different occasions.
pg063_n0031: For instance, festive decorations can evoke feelings of joy and celebration.
pg064_n0002: Social interaction: It can encourage social interaction or get-togethers.
pg064_n0003: Decorated homes or public places, for example, can bring people together to communicate and share experiences.
pg064_n0005: Cultural and historical Significance: It can preserve cultural and historical significance.
pg064_n0006: Traditional ornaments, symbols, or art facts can represent a personal, societal or national heritage and help keep cultural practices alive.
pg064_n0008: Steps in creating a simple decorative drawing
pg064_n0010: Simple decorative drawings require an artist to go through several processes to create them.
pg064_n0011: The processes include conception, analysis of the idea, planning, and production as discussed below:
pg064_n0013: Concept development: This is the initial stage where the artist comes up with the idea for the decorative drawing.
pg064_n0014: It involves brainstorming and visualising what the final piece will look like.
pg064_n0015: Artists can be inspired by both natural and non-natural sources.
pg064_n0016: The place where the decoration is going to be done also has a big role in influencing the type of decoration.
pg064_n0017: For example, animal images cannot be used for decoration in hospitals.
pg064_n0019: Analysis of idea: At this stage, the artist has to analyse the inspired idea to get the most of interest.
pg064_n0020: Then, the artist has to create preliminary sketches of the types of decoration images to be drawn.
pg064_n0022: Planning: This involves a decision on the material, equipment to be used, the size of the place and image, techniques to be used and any other necessary information like the location of the place and other technical aspects.
pg064_n0023: The artist may also create preliminary sketches during this stage.
pg064_n0025: Production: This is the final stage where the artist draws the decoration according to the prepared plans.

pg069_n0007: Painting is a form of fine art which involves the creation of images with colours.
pg069_n0008: Different societies in the world practice and embrace painting for its ability to express our inner thoughts, feelings, and experiences as creative beings.
pg069_n0009: When painting you can see that it is closely related to other forms of fine art such as drawing and design.
pg069_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of painting, materials and equipment for painting, colour theory, watercolour painting and approaches to painting, creating simple decorative paintings and painting by using traditional colours from the surroundings.
pg069_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to create and produce simple quality paintings using different techniques.
pg069_n0018: Painting is a form of fine art in which ideas, thoughts, emotions, and feelings are creatively expressed by using images in colours.
pg069_n0019: The work of art made from painting is also called a painting.
pg069_n0020: Painting can be made by using brushes and colours on surfaces such as walls, paper and canvas.
pg069_n0021: Painting is among the oldest and most famous forms of fine art.
pg069_n0022: Painting has always been practised alongside drawing, design and sculpture.
pg069_n0026: In fine art, the materials for painting a work of art are known as media.
pg069_n0027: In painting, the term media or medium means paints or colours that are used by artists when painting.
pg069_n0028: Paints are made of three components, namely pigment, binder and solvent.
pg069_n0029: The pigment is a fine ground, a coloured powder that gives paint its colour or hue.
pg069_n0030: The pigment is the main substance in the paint.
pg069_n0031: The pigment is made from animal remains, plants, rocks, minerals and soils.

pg070_n0006: liquid to which the dry pigment is added.
pg070_n0008: In painting, linseed oil is used to liquefy paint and make it glossy.
pg070_n0009: While a solvent is a liquid used to dissolve paint.
pg070_n0010: For example, turpentine, linseed oil and kerosene are solvents for oil paints, while water is a solvent for watercolours.
pg070_n0011: Solvents are also used to clean brushes.
pg070_n0012: Paint is the main medium for painting which is available in various packages such as in tubes, tins, powder or plastic containers.
pg070_n0013: Paints are categorised based on the kind of solvent they use.
pg070_n0014: These include; oil paints, watercolours, acrylics, gouache, and tempera.
pg070_n0016: Oil paint: This is an oil-based paint.
pg070_n0017: It was first used in the fourteen hundreds and has continued to be one of the most popular media of painting applied globally.
pg070_n0019: Watercolour: This is a painting medium in which the pigment is blended with water.
pg070_n0020: Watercolour is the most sensitive of all the painting media because it dries quickly.
pg070_n0021: It also reacts to the slightest touch of the artist and can become an overworked mess in a moment if not used carefully.
pg070_n0023: Acrylic: This is a quick-drying water-based synthetic paint, it is a manufactured paint with plastic binders.
pg070_n0024: Acrylic is very versatile and can be applied in both thick and thin glaze.
pg070_n0025: Once it is dried it becomes resistant to water.
pg070_n0027: Gouache is an opaque watercolour medium made of natural pigment with gum Arabic or dextrin binder.
pg070_n0028: It can be diversely used in making a range of artworks including murals illustrations and comics.
pg070_n0030: Tempera: This is a painting medium in which the pigment is mixed with egg yolk and water.
pg070_n0031: Tempera is a very old medium which has been used for thousands of years.
pg070_n0032: For instance, in the early Christian art era, tempera was used extensively to paint images of religious icons.
pg070_n0036: Equipment for painting means tools or instruments that are used in the painting activities.
pg070_n0039: Painting brushes: These are brushes used to apply paint or colour on the surface of a paper, board or canvas.
pg070_n0040: There are different sizes and shapes of brushes.
pg070_n0041: The shape and size of a brush is important because each brush is made for particular type and size of colour stroke.

pg070_n0045: This is because they are made to work with varieties of colours such as tempera, oil colours, acrylics and watercolours, without getting easily broken or diminished.

pg071_n0013: Most palettes are made of plastic, wood or aluminium materials.

pg072_n0006: Painting materials and equipment require proper handling for general safety.
pg072_n0007: Several rules need to be observed wherever one has painting materials and equipment.
pg072_n0008: The following general rules and procedures should be adhered to for the safety of materials, equipment and user or artist:
pg072_n0012: Artists should read user guides on art materials and equipment labels carefully before using them for the first time.
pg072_n0015: Warnings and precautions on painting materials and equipment labels should be strictly observed.
pg072_n0018: Paint containers and tubes should be tightly covered when not in use.
pg072_n0021: All material containers must be labelled.
pg072_n0022: For example, solvent containers should be labelled to avoid confusion in use.
pg072_n0023: If the water container is not labelled it can easily be confused with other odourless and colourless solvents.
pg072_n0026: Brushes and other art equipment should be properly cleaned, dried and kept in their cases instead of leaving them with paint or soaked in a solvent container after use.
pg072_n0027: This is due to the following reasons: It helps to maintain the quality of the equipment and prolong its lifespan.
pg072_n0028: It prevents the build-up of paint, ink, or other materials that can cause damage to the equipment overtime, it helps to prevent contamination of the materials used in the artwork.

pg073_n0025: When objects, things, and other living organisms are exposed to light, we see colours on them.
pg073_n0026: Therefore, colour is what we see on objects or things in light.
pg073_n0027: When you mix, match, compare or contrast colours you apply science.
pg073_n0028: When you creatively apply colours to communicate or express ideas, thoughts and feelings you practically create art.
pg073_n0032: Artists paint in different ways and techniques to achieve the desired qualities in their creations.
pg073_n0033: A good understanding of types of colours and their basic properties helps them to achieve a proper colour application, when painting to achieve desired results.
pg073_n0034: This part explains three main properties of colours.
pg073_n0035: These properties are hue, value and intensity.
pg073_n0038: This refers to colour in its original form.
pg073_n0039: It is a unique property or attribute of a certain colour quality.
pg073_n0040: For example, blue, red and yellow are attributes of a colour.
pg073_n0043: This is the quality of value lightness or darkness of a colour.
pg073_n0044: When working on hues, value can be altered by adding black or white.
pg073_n0045: The addition of black medium to a hue increases dark or black value, called a shade in colour.
pg073_n0046: Likewise, an addition of white medium to a colour adds a whiter or lighter value called a tint.
pg073_n0049: This is the Quality of brightness or dullness of a colour.
pg073_n0050: The intensity of the colour is also known as Chroma or Saturation.
pg073_n0051: The intensity of colour is a
pg074_n0005: The processes occur when colours are applied in the painting.
pg074_n0006: The brightness of colour is termed high intensity while the dullness is low intensity.
pg074_n0008: Note: The terms intensity and value, can be used interchangeably but they are not similar.
pg074_n0009: The difference between them is that value is changed or adjusted by adding black or white to a hue while intensity is changed by mixing a colour with its complementary in the colour wheel or grey colour.
pg074_n0013: A colour wheel is an illustrative arrangement of colours in a circle which is intended to show the relationship between colours.
pg074_n0014: A colour wheel helps to understand the origins of different colours.
pg074_n0015: In the wheel, some colours are natural and others are made by mixing two or more natural colours.
pg074_n0019: There are three groups of colours regarding their formation or origin.
pg074_n0020: These are; primary, secondary and tertiary or intermediate colours.
pg074_n0023: Red, yellow and blue are primary colours or hues.
pg074_n0024: They are equally placed in the colour wheel.
pg074_n0025: Primary colours are made or extracted from nature, such as minerals and plants.
pg074_n0026: These colours can be mixed in varying proportions to produce all other colours.
pg074_n0027: However, they cannot be made by mixing any other colours.

pg074_n0033: These are colours made by mixing an equal amount of two primary colours.
pg074_n0034: These secondary colours are purple, orange and green.

pg075_n0006: Secondary colours are normally arranged in between the primary colours in a colour wheel.
pg075_n0007: This arrangement illustrates primarily that when two primary colours are mixed they normally form a secondary colour.

pg076_n0002: Tertiary or intermediate colours: These are colours made by mixing a primary with its neighbouring secondary colour.
pg076_n0003: Tertiary colours that are made in this process include blue-green, blue-purple, red-purple, red-orange, yellow-orange, and yellow-green.

pg077_n0005: Tertiary colours are normally arranged in between primary and secondary colours in the colour wheel.
pg077_n0006: This arrangement illustrates which primary colours when mixed with secondary colours form tertiary colours.

pg077_n0013: An arrangement or combination of colours and their relationship on visibility is known as the colour scheme.
pg077_n0014: Colour schemes are used to create uniqueness and enhance visual attraction.
pg077_n0015: The major colour schemes are monochromatic, analogous, complementary, cool and warm colours.
pg077_n0018: These are colours arranged side by side with primary colours on a colour wheel.
pg077_n0019: For example, violet, red, red violet and red-orange are both analogous colours which share the same hue red base.
pg077_n0022: Warm colours are those colours that suggest a warm feeling.
pg077_n0023: These include red, yellow and orange.
pg077_n0024: Cool colours such as green, blue and purple create a sense of calmness and coldness.
pg077_n0025: Usually, they are creatively used to evoke relaxation or calm feelings in art.
pg077_n0026: Figure three point nine shows warm and cool colours.
pg077_n0029: These are colours which are opposite to each other on the colour wheel.
pg077_n0030: Yellow and purple, orange and blue, yellow-green and red-purple, and red and green are complementary colours.

pg078_n0010: Monochromatic colours: These are all colours of the same hue but different values after tinting or shading.
pg078_n0011: For example, blue, dark blue, medium blue and light blue are a good set of monochromatic blue schemes.
pg078_n0012: The term monochrome originates from Greek.
pg078_n0014: Monochrome means varieties of a single colour or hue.

pg079_n0025: Watercolour painting is the process of applying water-based colours on a surface.
pg079_n0026: There are several types of watercolour paints that an artist can use in painting.
pg079_n0027: These include tube, liquid and dry cake or pan watercolours.
pg079_n0028: Tube watercolours are paints in metal or plastic tubes whereas liquid watercolours consist of pigments suspended in water base solution stored in tins or cans.
pg079_n0029: Dry cake or pan watercolours come in the form of dry cakes in small plastic pans that require more water to make them stable for painting.
pg079_n0030: Other watercolours come in the form of coloured pencils and crayons.
pg079_n0031: Water soluble coloured pencils produce a different effect when applied dry.
pg079_n0035: Using watercolours to paint is very challenging because it dries very fast as a result mixing layers becomes difficult.
pg079_n0036: Watercolour layers also spread easily and controlling borders is difficult.
pg079_n0037: One needs a lot of practice to master applying watercolour painting techniques.
pg079_n0038: Painting techniques such as wet-on-dry, wet-on-wet, wash and dry-on-dry need a lot of practice before applying them in actual painting.
pg079_n0041: This is a technique of applying a wet paintbrush on dry paper.
pg079_n0042: It is suitable for adding details and giving the painting sharp clean edges.
pg079_n0045: This is a technique almost similar to the wet-on-dry technique except that in wet-on-wet paint is applied on wet paper instead of dry paper.
pg079_n0046: This technique is often applied in painting to blend colours.
pg079_sec001_ans_item-1: A colour wheel is a circular arrangement of colours that shows the relationship between primary, secondary and tertiary colours.
pg079_sec001_ans_item-2: A colour scheme is the planned combination or arrangement of colours used in an artwork or design.
pg079_sec001_ans_item-3: Complementary colours are colours that are opposite each other on the colour wheel and they create strong contrast when placed together.
pg079_sec001_ans_item-4: Tertiary colours are colours formed by mixing a primary colour with a neighbouring secondary colour.
pg079_sec001_ans_item-5: Secondary colours are formed by mixing two primary colours, for example red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and red and blue make violet. Tertiary colours are formed by mixing a primary colour with a secondary colour next to it on the colour wheel.
pg080_n0005: Wash technique: It is a technique of applying the paint evenly on a dry or wet paper surface.
pg080_n0006: Wash is used to develop a background on a painted image and show consistency.
pg080_n0007: This technique can be practised using one or more colours.
pg080_n0009: Dry-on-dry technique: This is a technique where a dry brush with very little paint is lightly and quickly streaked across a dry piece of paper.
pg080_n0010: This technique is suitable for adding details to a painting, for example, when detailing furs on a dog, leaves of a tree or long hairs on a girl’s head.
pg080_n0014: Colours have several functions when applied in art.
pg080_n0015: Artists use colours to decorate environments, communicate messages and enhance forms of work of art.
pg080_n0016: The following are the common uses of colour in art;
pg080_n0020: Colours are used to enhance object recognition and visibility: We recognise objects more quickly when their colours reflect what we see in the real world.
pg080_n0023: Colours can be used to symbolise something of a cultural value.
pg080_n0026: Colours can be used in the expression of emotions and feelings.
pg080_n0027: Artists use colours to communicate their thoughts, ideas and feelings.
pg080_n0028: For instance, warm colours like red, orange and yellow evoke warmth, passion and energy while cool colours like blue, green and purple represent calmness, peace and relaxation.
pg080_n0029: Additionally, an artist can use colours to convey their feelings or communicate wider social and cultural ideas we associate with certain colours.
pg080_n0032: Colours can be used to influence or guide the way a work of art is appreciated by the audience.
pg080_n0035: Colours are used to put emphasis on some parts of the work of art as well as to attract attention of the viewers to the artist’s work.

pg081_n0018: Artists obtain their paintings subject matter either from memory, imagination or observation.
pg081_n0019: When an artist decides on the source of his content, he or she makes sketches about the ideas, thoughts, feelings or imagination and prepares all necessary tools and equipment for his work.
pg081_n0020: Similarly, the artist makes or preparations, when painting from direct observation of nature or experience.
pg081_n0022: Painting from memory: This is an approach to painting in which a work of art is made to depict bits and pieces of images of a subject recalled or memorised from past experiences.
pg081_n0023: When painting from memory, it becomes very difficult to compare the source of the work of art to its results.
pg081_n0025: Painting from imagination: This is a little different to painting from memory except all that an artist is creating in the final artwork is not a representation of anything existed before.
pg081_n0026: Imaginative painting is made of images, shapes, and colour schemes from scratch, based on visualised ideas in the mind of the artist.
pg081_n0028: Painting from observation: This is an approach that artists use when they want to paint a subject or an object correctly but not precisely.
pg081_n0029: This approach is applied to other approaches such as still-life painting.
pg081_n0030: It involves observing various subjects, such as landscapes, seascapes, animals, plants and even still life set up.
pg081_n0031: The difference between painting from observation and still life painting is on representational attributes of a still life approach which are not necessary in the painting from observation.
pg081_n0033: Still life painting: It is a style of painting involving arranged inanimate objects which are displayed over a flat surface or a table.
pg081_n0034: The artist is supposed to produce an exact copy of objects displayed in the form of a painted picture.

pg088_n0005: Procedures for extracting colours from flowers
pg088_n0007: An artist is required to follow the following procedures in extracting colours from flowers:
pg088_n0009: Gathering the flower petals of different colours: Collect the fresh flowers and carefully pick the petals off each stem and separate them into bowls according to the petals' colours.
pg088_n0011: Use hot water: Pour a small amount of hot water over petals in each bowl and stir them to release the colour.
pg088_n0012: You may use a wooden spoon to stir the petals.
pg088_n0014: Alter the shades: Squeeze a small amount of lemon to lighten the colours and bicarbonate of soda to darken them.
pg088_n0015: The acidity of the lemon will alter the p h of the colour and take it to almost neon levels, whilst the bicarbonate of soda will make the dye more alkaline and deepen the colour.

pg090_n0028: Procedures for extracting colours from soil
pg090_n0030: The following are the procedures for extracting colours from soil:
pg090_n0033: Collect soil of different colours from different places and separate it into bowls based on the colours.
pg090_n0036: Remove all unnecessary particles, allow the soil to dry and crush it to get a powder form.
pg090_n0039: Pour the powder into the bowls, add water and glue and mix it well to get a smooth mixture.
pg090_n0040: It is now ready for use.

pg090_n0046: Apply several layers of the painting one after the other and allow them to dry.

pg091_n0038: Procedures for extracting colours from fruits and roots
pg091_n0040: Fruits and roots are good sources of natural colours.
pg091_n0041: The colours can be obtained from tomatoes, ripe mangoes, carrots and various other roots.
pg092_n0004: Collecting fruits and roots of different colours: These collections depend on the type of colour needed from the fruits and roots.
pg092_n0005: Separate the fruits and roots into bowls based on their colours.
pg092_n0007: Fruits and roots: Clean the fruits and roots to reveal their natural colour, and blend them to get a smooth heavy juice.
pg092_n0008: Clean all unnecessary particles and crush them to get small particles.
pg092_n0010: Use water: Pour the small particles of fruits or roots into the bowls, add water and glue into each, and mix them well to get the colour you need.
pg092_n0012: Procedures for using natural colours from the surroundings to paint
pg092_n0014: The following are procedures for using natural colours from the surroundings to paint:
pg092_n0016: Identify sources of natural colours: Look around your school environment, or go for a nature walk to find colourful materials like flowers, leaves, fruits and roots that can be used to make paints.
pg092_n0018: Gather the materials: Pick a few fallen leaves, flowers, fruits and roots.
pg092_n0019: It is advised that you should not harm living plants or the environment.
pg092_n0021: Drying and crushing the materials: After gathering the materials, allow them to air dry for one or two days.
pg092_n0022: Once they are dry, crush and grind them properly into fine granules.
pg092_n0024: Add a binder: Mix a little bit of water with the crushed pigment to make a paste.
pg092_n0025: This paste helps the colour stick to our paper or canvas.
pg092_n0027: Test the colours: Dip your paintbrush into the natural paint and try it on a piece of paper.
pg092_n0028: Observe how beautiful the colours are.
pg092_n0030: Create different colours: To make different colours, try to mix different pigments.
pg092_n0031: For example, mix red and blue pigments to get purple.
pg092_n0033: Paint a picture: Now that you have your natural paint, use it to paint various pictures.
pg092_n0035: Storing the paint: If you have any remaining paints, you can keep them in small containers with lids.
pg092_n0036: Make sure to label the colours on each container.

pg096_n0009: Printmaking is part and parcel of our life.
pg096_n0010: It offers huge value to our daily life as it allows images and texts to be reproduced.
pg096_n0011: Every sector of our life is full of printmaking.
pg096_n0012: The clothes we wear are mostly products of printmaking, our books and every business advertisement we see all over hanging in streets in the form of posters and billboards are made possible because of printmaking.
pg096_n0013: It helps us to feel comfortable and enjoy life.
pg096_n0014: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of printmaking with focus on meaning, techniques, materials, tools and equipment used in printmaking and creating simple decorative monoprints.
pg096_n0015: The competencies developed will enable you to create and produce simple prints which will then make you an entrepreneur in printmaking activities.
pg096_n0018: Printing products and their significance worldwide
pg096_n0022: Printmaking is an artistic process based on the principle of transferring images from a matrix onto another surface, most often paper or fabric.
pg096_n0023: A print is an artwork made up of ink on a flat surface such as canvas, paper, fabric and cups.
pg096_n0024: The plate is where you transfer and create the original image to print multiple copies.
pg096_n0025: The process is not created by painting or drawing images on a surface, but pressing the paper to an inked surface of the image.
pg096_n0026: Printmaking is developed to help artists get more copies of the original artwork within a few times.
pg096_n0027: For example, an artist can manage to print five hundred T-shirts for a particular campaign within a day through the printmaking process.
pg096_n0028: Such a task could take longer if other methods like painting or drawing are used.
pg096_n0029: Printmaking is also used to make rubber stamps, print on complex areas like high-height walls and decorate fabrics like table covers, curtains and bed sheets.
pg096_n0030: Printmaking is done in different ways and techniques.
pg097_n0006: Printmaking can be done through various techniques.
pg097_n0007: Some of them include stencil, relief, intaglio and screen printing.
pg097_n0011: A stencil uses a thin sheet of hard paper or plastic with a design to be cut on it and printed.
pg097_n0012: These can be used to produce the cut design on the surface it is placed.
pg097_n0013: The process is done through applying ink or paint on the stencil, either by using spray paint or opaque paint in which a sponge or brush can be used.
pg097_n0014: Then, the pigment penetrates through the stencil holes to allow motif patterns to appear on the design.
pg097_n0015: Figure four point one indicates a prepared stencil while Figure four point two, a, and Figure four point two, b, show the printing process through stencil method.
pg097_n0019: The materials, tools, and equipment used for stencil printing are:
pg097_n0021: Stencil film: This is a hard paper or plastic used to create a stencil.
pg097_n0022: The cut design is set on it.
pg097_n0024: Carving knife: This is a flat sharp-edged metal used to cut out the design from a stencil film.
pg097_n0026: Masking tape: This is made of thin paper used to stick together stencils and paper to be printed.
pg097_n0028: Printing ink: This is a fluid or paste used for printing on a surface.
pg097_n0029: When they are used, they leave a particular mark on a design.
pg097_n0031: Squeegee: It is a tool used for evenly applying ink to the stencil.
pg097_n0033: Printing papers: These are specialised printmaking papers which are used for relief printing.
pg097_n0034: They are chosen for their ability to hold ink well and produce high-quality prints.
pg097_n0035: The thickness and texture of the paper can influence the final appearance of the print.
pg097_n0037: Printing table: A flat and stable surface for inking and stencil printing.

pg100_n0006: Relief printing is the process of producing a relief print.
pg100_n0007: A relief print is an image produced by a raised surface from the block plate.
pg100_n0008: The completed carved design is inked by using a roller then transferred to an intended place by applying pressure to the entire plate evenly.
pg100_n0009: In most cases, relief printing is done by using woodcut and linocut.
pg100_n0010: However, artists can improvise other accessible and available materials.
pg100_n0012: Relief printing involves several processes including creating an image for printing, transferring the image and cutting the plate to reveal an intended image to be printed.
pg100_n0013: An intended image is first drawn on a flat plate.
pg100_n0014: The printing plate in relief printing is created by removing, or deleting, areas that are not intended to be printed, or in other words, remove the background so that it remains white during the printing process.
pg100_n0015: The remaining areas of the original surface receive the ink.
pg100_n0016: It is a printing process whereby areas that you do not want to print are physically removed.
pg100_n0017: The remaining raised areas are inked and printed.
pg100_n0018: Relief printing can be done by hand or a printing press.
pg100_n0022: There are various materials used in relief printing as discussed here:
pg100_n0025: This is sometimes known as printing block.
pg100_n0026: It is the most critical material in relief printing.
pg100_n0027: It can be made from various materials, including:
pg100_n0030: Woodblocks are commonly used, and different types of wood, like linoleum, plywood, or hardwood, can be chosen based on the desired results.
pg100_n0033: Also known as lino-cut, linoleum blocks are softer and easier to carve than woodblocks, making them popular for beginners and artists looking for a quicker process.
pg100_n0036: Rubber blocks or soft sculpture blocks offer a flexible and easy-to-carve surface.
pg100_n0038: Other materials an artist can improvise include potatoes, cassava, or linoleum.
pg100_n0041: Relief printmakers use various tools to carve the block and create the image.
pg100_n0042: Some of these include carving knives, chisels, trimming knives, sandpapers, razorblades, and any other related carving tools.
pg101_n0006: Printing ink: Printing ink for relief printing is usually oil-based or water-based and comes in various colours.
pg101_n0007: Oil-based inks are more traditional, take longer to dry, and are often used when printing on paper.
pg101_n0008: Water-based inks are more suitable for beginners, as they are easier to clean up and dry faster.
pg101_n0010: Printing paper: Specialised printmaking papers are used for relief printing.
pg101_n0011: They are chosen for their ability to hold ink well and produce high-quality prints.
pg101_n0012: The thickness and texture of the paper can influence the final appearance of the print.
pg101_n0014: Tools and equipment used in relief printing
pg101_n0016: Relief printing often shares most of the same tools and materials used by other printing techniques.
pg101_n0019: Brayer: A brayer, also known as an ink roller, is used to apply ink evenly to the surface of the block.
pg101_n0020: It ensures that the ink is distributed smoothly, hence, achieve consistent and clean prints.
pg101_n0022: Printing press: Using a printing press can provide even pressure and help achieve more consistent prints, especially when working with large editions.
pg101_n0024: Printing table: This is a flat and stable surface for inking and printing the blocks.
pg101_n0026: Baren: A handheld tool used to apply pressure when hand-printing relief prints, especially useful for small-scale works.
pg101_n0028: Protective gear: Relief printmaking can involve the use of sharp tools, so wearing gloves and eye protection is recommended to ensure safety during the carving process.

pg101_n0035: For example, it can be a symbol, flower, animal, or anything requested by your teacher.
pg101_n0037: Transfer the completed drawn image: There are several methods an image can be transferred from a sketchbook to a relief printmaking plate.

pg103_n0026: Intaglio printing is a traditional printing process used to produce high-quality images or designs on paper, currency, postage stamps, and other valuable documents.
pg103_n0027: The term “intaglio” comes from the Italian word for “engraved” or “cut in,” which accurately describes the key characteristic of this printing method.
pg103_n0028: The intaglio printing process is known for its ability to produce fine details, rich tones, and high-quality prints, making it particularly suitable for printing banknotes, security documents, and valuable art prints.
pg103_n0029: The complexity and craftsmanship involved in intaglio printing also make it difficult to copy.
pg103_n0030: This has contributed to its use in anti-counterfeiting measures for currency and other important documents.

pg104_n0007: Materials used in the intaglio printing process
pg104_n0009: Intaglio printing requires specific materials, tools, and equipment to create the engraved plates and produce the final prints.
pg104_n0010: The key items used in the intaglio printing process are:
pg104_n0012: Metal plates: Copper, zinc, or steel plates are commonly used as the base material for intaglio printing.
pg104_n0013: Copper is the most traditional choice due to its malleability and excellent ink retention properties.
pg104_n0015: Printing ink: Specialised intaglio printing inks are used.
pg104_n0016: These inks are typically oil-based and have a higher viscosity to ensure they stick well to the engraved lines and grooves on the plate.
pg104_n0018: Printing paper: High-quality, dampened paper is used for the printing process.
pg104_n0019: The paper should be able to withstand the pressure applied during printing and effectively absorb the ink from the plate.
pg104_n0021: Tools and equipment used in intaglio printing process
pg104_n0023: The following are tools and equipment used in intaglio printing press:
pg105_n0005: Etching needle: An etching needle is a pointed tool used for creating fine lines and details on the metal plate during the engraving process.
pg105_n0007: Burin: A burin is a specialised engraving tool with a sharp, V-shaped tip.
pg105_n0008: It is used to incise broader lines and remove metal from the plate to create shaded areas.
pg105_n0010: Roulette: This is a small, spiked wheel-like tool used to create a random texture or pattern on the plate.
pg105_n0011: This technique is often used in backgrounds or areas where shading is required.
pg105_n0013: Scraper slash burnisher: The scraper is used to remove excess ink from the plate during the wiping process, while the burnisher is used to smoothen and polish the surface of the plate before printing.
pg105_n0015: Intaglio printing press: This is a heavy-duty printing press specifically designed for intaglio printing.
pg105_n0016: The press exerts significant pressure to transfer the ink from the engraved plate to the paper.
pg105_n0018: Wiping cloth slash pads: These kinds of cloths or pads are used for wiping excess ink from the plate, leaving ink only in the engraved lines and grooves.
pg105_n0020: Dampening system: A system to moisten the printing paper, ensuring it remains damp during the printing process.
pg105_n0021: This enhances the paper’s ability to pick up the ink from the plate.
pg105_n0023: Drying racks: Used to lay out and dry the freshly printed sheets of paper.
pg105_n0027: The intaglio printing process involves the following steps:
pg105_n0029: Plate preparation: A metal plate, typically made of copper, zinc, or steel, is meticulously prepared for engraving.
pg105_n0030: Its surface is polished and cleaned to ensure a smooth and even base.
pg105_n0032: Engraving: Skilled artisans, known as engravers or etchers, use specialised tools to cut or incise the image into the plate’s surface.
pg105_n0033: This process involves creating fine lines and varying depths to represent different tones and shades in the final print.
pg105_n0034: The engraved plate becomes the master image that will be transferred onto the paper.
pg106_n0002: Inking: Ink is applied to the entire surface of the engraved plate.
pg106_n0003: Since the plate is wiped clean after inking, the ink only remains in the incised lines and grooves.
pg106_n0005: Wiping: The surface of the plate is carefully wiped to remove excess ink, leaving ink only in the engraved areas.
pg106_n0007: Printing: A dampened sheet of high-quality paper is placed on the inked plate, and pressure is applied to transfer the ink from the plate to the paper.
pg106_n0008: This pressure is usually applied using a roller press or an intaglio printing press, which forces the paper into the incised lines, picking up the ink.
pg106_n0009: This results in a high level of detail and depth in the final print.
pg106_n0011: Drying: The printed paper is left to dry thoroughly before any further processing or handling.

pg106_n0022: Screen printing is widely used for a variety of applications, including t-shirts, posters, signage, textiles, electronics, and more.
pg106_n0023: Its ability to print on various surfaces, along with the vibrant colours and durability of the prints, makes it a favoured choice for many printing projects.

pg107_n0007: Tools used in screen printing process
pg107_n0009: Screen printing requires a specific set of tools and materials to create the stencils and apply ink onto the printing surface.
pg107_n0010: Here are the key tools and materials used in the screen-printing process:
pg107_n0012: Screen: The screen is the most essential tool in screen printing.
pg107_n0013: It is typically made of a frame and a tightly stretched mesh.
pg107_n0014: The choice of mesh material, for example polyester or nylon, depends on the printing application and the type of ink.
pg107_n0016: Squeegee: A squeegee is a handheld tool with a rubber or polyurethane blade that is used to push ink through the open areas of the screen and onto the printing surface.
pg107_n0018: Printing press: A screen printing press holds the screen firmly in place and allows precise and consistent printing.
pg107_n0019: There are various types of presses, including manual and automatic.
pg107_n0021: Exposure unit: An exposure unit is used to expose the screen to U V light after the design has been applied to the emulsion.
pg107_n0022: This hardens the emulsion in the areas not blocked by the design, and as a result, the stencil is created.
pg107_n0024: Washout booth or sink: After exposure, the screen needs to be washed to remove the unhardened emulsion.
pg107_n0025: A washout booth or sink equipped with water and possibly a pressure washer is used for this purpose.
pg107_n0027: Drying racks: Drying racks are used to store and dry freshly printed materials without smudging the ink.
pg108_n0005: Materials used in screen printing process
pg108_n0007: The following are materials used in the screen-printing process:
pg108_n0009: Screen mesh: The mesh is available in different thread counts or mesh counts per inch, which affects the level of detail that can be achieved in the print.
pg108_n0010: The mesh count is chosen based on the artwork’s complexity and the type of ink being used.
pg108_n0012: Emulsion: Emulsion is a light-sensitive liquid applied to the screen mesh.
pg108_n0013: It becomes solid when exposed to U V light, creating the stencil.
pg108_n0015: Transparent film or vellum: The design is printed on transparent film or vellum, which is used to transfer the artwork onto the emulsion-coated screen during exposure.
pg108_n0017: Screen printing ink: Screen printing inks come in various types, including water-based, plastisol, and discharge inks.
pg108_n0018: The choice of ink depends on the printing surface, for example fabric or paper, and the desired effect, for example opaque, soft, or vibrant colours.
pg108_n0020: Substrate: The material being printed on, such as fabric, paper, glass, metal, or plastic, is known as the substrate.
pg108_n0022: Clean-up supplies: Various chemicals and solvents are used for cleaning the screen, removing excess ink, and reclaiming screens for reuse.
pg108_n0024: Registration guides: These guides help align different colour layers precisely during multicolour printing, ensuring that the final design looks sharp and well-defined.
pg108_n0026: Note: A motif used in the screen method should be printed with heavy and quality ink.
pg108_n0027: Kerosene or any cooking oil must be available, as it helps to moisten a screen motif on paper, making it easy to transfer the motif from paper to the screen.
pg108_n0028: The mixing ratio of a photo emulsion is to some extent estimation, but the simple estimation is as follows; one teaspoonful of sensitiser should be mixed and dissolved in five hundred millilitres of water by shaking well to let the sensitiser dissolve in water.
pg108_n0029: Then take five teaspoons of photo emulsion plus two teaspoons of sensitizer.
pg109_n0006: Steps in creating a mesh screen
pg109_n0008: The following are steps in creating a mesh screen:
pg109_n0012: Create a frame by using pieces of wood, then bind the mesh on it.
pg109_n0015: Mix photo emulsion with a little amount of sensitiser, then stir the mixture.
pg109_n0016: This should be done in a dark place.
pg109_n0019: Pick a photo emulsion by using a squeegee, then apply it on the mesh screen, in a dark room.
pg109_n0022: Dry the mesh screen using a heat gun, drier or fan, and leave it for a moment to let the screen dry.
pg109_n0025: Take a motif on printed paper and attach it to the back side of the mesh screen.
pg109_n0026: The motif should face the mesh screen.
pg109_n0027: The image of the motif should be touching the mesh screen then, pour kerosene on the paper motif in a dark place.
pg109_n0030: Place a transparent mirror on the screen mesh behind the paper motif and tight both the mirror, the paper motif and the screen mesh.
pg109_n0033: Expose the combination of mesh, the motif and the mirror on the required light.
pg109_n0034: Remember, the transparent mirror should face the light from two minutes to ten minutes.
pg109_n0035: But it depends on the amount of source of light and the mixture of photo emulsion.
pg109_n0038: Separate the mirror and the motif paper from the screen, then clean the screen slowly by using a sponge and water.
pg109_n0039: Once a motif is visible on the screen, use the spray gun to wash the screen until the motif is seen.
pg109_n0042: Dry the screen using a heat gun or sunlight.
pg109_n0044: Note, in case the motif does not appear on the screen mesh, it is likely that the sensitizer is excessive in the photo emulsion or the time of exposing it to light rays has been insufficient.
pg109_n0045: The solution to such a problem is either to add a sensitizer in photo emulsion or increase exposure to light rays.
pg109_n0047: Printing procedures using a mesh screen
pg109_n0049: The steps to create the screen for printing are well described above, now, the printing process can be executed without any problem.
pg109_n0050: Observe the following steps of using a created screen to print an impression on a chosen surface.
pg110_n0003: Set up your printing area: Lay down old newspapers or cardboard to protect your work surface from ink spills.
pg110_n0005: Setup and registration: The screen is mounted onto the screen-printing press, which holds it securely in place.
pg110_n0006: Proper registration is crucial, as it ensures that each colour layer aligns perfectly with the others in the final print.
pg110_n0008: Ink application: A specific ink is applied to its respective screen.
pg110_n0009: A squeegee is used to spread the ink over the open areas of the screen, pushing the ink through the mesh and onto the printing surface.
pg110_n0011: Printing process: The printer pulls the squeegee across the screen, pushing the ink through the mesh and onto the material being printed.
pg110_n0012: This process is repeated for each colour layer, allowing the ink to overlap and create the full-colour design.
pg110_n0014: Curing: Once the printing is complete, the printed material is typically passed through a curing unit or oven.
pg110_n0015: This process cures the ink, making it more durable and resistant to fading or washing out.
pg110_n0017: Clean-up: After printing, the screen needs to be thoroughly cleaned to remove any remaining ink and emulsion, allowing it to be reused for future printing works.

pg111_n0010: This is a printmaking method that creates simple, unique and one-of-a-kind images specifically as a straightforward decoration artwork.
pg111_n0011: It involves creating an image on a flat surface, like a plate or a piece of glass, and then transferring it to paper or another medium by using ink.
pg111_n0012: Unlike traditional printmaking methods where multiple prints can be produced from the same plate, monoprints are essentially one-of-a-kind prints, hence the name “mono” meaning a single printing.
pg111_n0013: The process allows for experimentation and a wide range of artistic expression.
pg111_n0014: Here’s an overview of monoprinting techniques.
pg111_n0016: Materials used in the monoprint process
pg111_n0018: There are materials that are inevitable in the monoprinting process.
pg111_n0021: Printing plate: A flat surface on which the image is created.
pg111_n0022: It can be made of materials like plexiglas, metal, glass, or even a smooth, non-absorbent surface like acrylic.
pg111_n0024: Printing ink or paint: Artists can use printing inks specifically designed for printmaking or various types of paint suitable for the chosen technique, for example, acrylics for direct painting.
pg111_n0026: Printing paper: Specialised printmaking papers that are capable of absorbing the ink or paint and producing high quality prints.
pg111_n0028: Inking roller, Brayer: A rubber roller used to apply ink or paint to the printing plate evenly.
pg111_n0030: Palette or inking plate: A flat surface for rolling out and blending ink or paint.
pg111_n0032: Drawing tools: Pencils, brushes, or other mark-making tools to create the image on the printing plate.
pg112_n0003: Stencils and masks: Used to create defined shapes or patterns on the printing plate.
pg112_n0004: Textures and collage materials: Various materials like fabric, leaves, textured papers, or other objects can be added to the printing plate to create interesting textures and effects.
pg112_n0006: Tools and equipment in the monoprint process
pg112_n0008: The following are the tools and equipment used in the monoprinting process:
pg112_n0010: Printing press: While not always necessary for monoprinting, some artists may use a printing press to apply pressure evenly and ensure a consistent transfer of the image from the plate to the paper.
pg112_n0011: Baren: A hand-held tool used to apply pressure when hand-printing is done, especially useful for small scale works.
pg112_n0012: Printing registration system: For multi-layered monoprints, artists may use a registration system to ensure accurate alignment of different layers.
pg112_n0013: Cleaning supplies: Materials like rags, sponges, and solvents are used to clean the printing plate between prints or to create specific effects.
pg112_n0014: Protective gloves and apron: Essentially important when working with inks, paints, or cleaning solvents.
pg112_n0016: Processes of creating simple decorative monoprint
pg112_n0018: The artists have to design an interesting item to be printed.
pg112_n0019: The artist can get inspiration for decorative monoprints from a variety of interesting natural things like distinct textures, flowers, twigs, and places or events where the monoprint is going to be used.
pg112_n0020: Once the design is set, the following has to be done:
pg112_n0022: Set up the work area: Lay down newspapers or plastic sheets to protect your workspace from paint spills and smudges.
pg112_n0023: Surface preparation: Start by selecting a smooth, non-absorbent surface as your printing plate.
pg112_n0024: Common choices include acrylic sheets, plexiglass, or even a well-polished metal surface.
pg112_n0025: Ink or paint application: Squeeze a small amount of ink or water-based paint onto the palette.
pg112_n0026: You can use a single colour or experiment with a combination of colours to create unique effects.
pg113_n0004: Apply a thin and even layer of ink or paint directly on the surface of the plate.
pg113_n0005: Avoid using too much paint, as it may smudge the print.
pg113_n0006: You can use brayers, brushes, or other tools to spread the ink evenly across the plate.

pg118_n0008: Art in Tanzania encompasses various forms of artistic expression reflecting the country’s rich history, cultural, social, political, and economic status.
pg118_n0009: The art production ranges from simple to complex; that is from self-taught creative artists to skilled professionals, and includes a wide variety of genres.
pg118_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about art in Tanzania, the Tingatinga painting movement and the Makonde sculpture movement.
pg118_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to produce various artworks which then make you an entrepreneur in the world of art.
pg118_n0014: The influence of art on national identity
pg118_n0016: Concept of trends of art in Tanzania
pg118_n0018: Trends of art simply mean “tendencies in art” typically used to depict artistic latest development in terms of form, subject, style or any other aesthetic dimensions.
pg118_n0019: Tanzania, like other countries all over the world has experienced such tendencies all the time.
pg118_n0021: Between rock art painting and modern times, Tanzanian art has been evolving in styles.
pg118_n0022: Rock painting emerged through the ancient rock painters who lived during the Stone Age however, they managed to express their feelings and memories, through painting their life experiences which involved hunting and gathering.
pg118_n0023: The oldest paintings made during the Stone Age are found in the Kondoa Irangi rock shelters in the central regions of Tanzania, see Figure five point one.
pg118_n0024: Similar rock paintings were later discovered in several rock shelters surrounding Lake Victoria in the Mara and Mwanza regions.
pg118_n0026: Some of the main features of prehistoric rock paintings were the use of various geometrical patterns, and figures of fauna and flora painted on rock surfaces.
pg119_n0004: After this period, Tanzania went through two famous major visual art movements and schools.
pg119_n0005: The Tingatinga Painting School and the Modern Makonde Sculpture Movement have put Tanzania on the world art map.
pg119_n0007: The influence of Tanzania paintings and sculptures can be seen inside and outside the country.
pg119_n0008: Tanzanian artists also get ideas and inspiration from other countries or various regions of the country which develop distinctive artistic traditions.

pg120_n0006: The Tingatinga painting movement was originally introduced by a Tanzanian, Edward Said Tingatinga, who was born in nineteen thirty-two in Mindu village, Tunduru district, Ruvuma region.
pg120_n0007: This type of art is named by the founder’s name.
pg120_n0008: His earliest inspiration for painting started at Mindu village where mural painting in folk art tradition was part of his people’s cultural heritage.
pg120_n0009: The artists from Zaire, now D R C, who used to sell their artworks to foreigners in the curio shops of Dar es Salaam also inspired Tingatinga.
pg120_n0010: It was such inspiration that drove him into painting.
pg120_n0011: It was in Dar es Salaam in nineteen sixty-eight that Tingatinga started to paint after finding out that painting could generate some income.
pg120_n0013: Tingatinga met his tragic death through mistaken identity.
pg120_n0014: His taxi driver disobeyed a police order to stop, something which irritated the police patrol who started a car chase that resulted in a shootout that killed Edward Said Tingatinga.
pg120_n0016: Although Tingatinga died in May nineteen seventy-two, his followers continued to create several styles whose stylistic evolution continued to spread in other countries such as Kenya, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark.
pg120_n0017: Figure five point two shows Edward Said Tingatinga at work.
