pg120_n0022: In nineteen seventy-one The National Arts Council showcased Tingatinga’s works on a stand at the International Trade Fair, Sabasaba grounds in Dar es Salaam, where his paintings
pg121_n0004: then began to be known and highly demanded beyond Tanzania’s boundaries.
pg121_n0005: The sales of his artworks changed the economy of Edward Said Tingatinga.
pg121_n0006: Instantly, Tingatinga’s artwork gained popularity all over the world.
pg121_n0007: In nineteen seventy-four, two years after his death, the National Museum of Copenhagen, Denmark organised and held the first Tingatinga Painting Art Exhibition to take place outside Tanzania.
pg121_n0008: Now, Tingatinga is not alive but his works still speak and help our country to be recognised in the world.
pg121_n0009: The high demand for such kind of artworks in the market enhances their values and makes them be sold at high prices on the internet and other various platforms.
pg121_n0011: After his death, some of his close relatives and friends who became the first and second generation of Tingatinga painters, organised themselves and registered their centre as a cooperative, known as Tingatinga Art Cooperative Society, T A C S.
pg121_n0012: The centre enabled members to proceed doing what Tingatinga had started.
pg121_n0013: Currently, in the art field, there are more than one hundred Tingatinga artists, who still create more and new Tingatinga painting styles.
pg121_n0014: See Figure five point three and Figure five point four.
pg121_n0015: Tingatinga himself introduced the major style of Single object painting style, his followers evolved more styles such as the Maasai, Historia, Landscape.
pg121_n0016: Story-telling style, Mashetani, Cartoon, Zimbabwe, Kilimanjaro, Vipepeo, Samaki, Maua, Matunda, Vyumba, Panels, The Aboriginal Australian, Abstract, Mzuguno floral and more other styles.
pg121_n0018: The founder Edward Said Tingatinga, trained only five first apprentices of the school, most of whom were either his close relatives or friends.
pg121_n0019: These were Kasper Henrick Tedo, January John Linda, Adeus Manndu Mmatambwe, Abdalah Ajaba, and Simon George Mpata who was Tingatinga’s youngest brother.
pg121_n0020: After his death, intruders joined the school.
pg121_n0021: Some of these were the late Omari Amonde, his nephew, Mohamed Abas Charinda, George Lilanga, Hashim Mruta, Damian Msagula, and Said Chilamboni to mention only a few.
pg121_n0022: This group became the first generation of Tingatinga Painting School.
pg121_n0023: This generation reproduced the same works of their founder.
pg121_n0024: Later on, the first generation trained more apprentices, who were, Ally Wasia, Ramadhani Sarange, Said Mitole, and others.
pg121_n0025: These became the second generation of Tingatinga Painting School.
pg121_n0026: This emerged group introduced new styles in response to transformations of new subjects related to the new urban and malt-ethnic society of Dar es Salaam.
pg121_n0027: Examples of such new subjects were crowded and busy streets, the introduction of pictorial depth, and other fine art techniques, a situation which if the founder were alive, no one could have tried.
pg121_n0028: Currently, Tingatinga is no longer a family or a certain ethnic group’s painting style.
pg121_n0029: With such freedom of creativity, the school remains with its long-established informal rules of painting Tingatinga art works set by its founder.

pg127_n0006: Makonde sculpture originated from the Makonde people living on the plateau, south of the Ruvuma river in Mozambique.
pg127_n0007: These people migrated northward into Tanzania and joined the curio trade that began to emerge in the nineteen fifties and nineteen sixties in Mtwara and Dar es Salaam.
pg127_n0008: Traditionally, the Makonde people create household together with ritual objects such as masks used in initiation ceremonies.
pg127_n0009: The contemporary Makonde artists create sculptures for business purposes rather than for society’s use.
pg127_n0010: Makonde sculptures are carved from the ebony hardwood which is known as mpingo in Swahili language.
pg127_n0011: The mpingo wood is characterised by black colour.
pg127_n0012: However, other wood such as mpolopolo, mwarobaini and mninga, just to mention a few, are used to create sculptures.
pg127_n0013: Makonde sculptures are not only popular in Tanzania but in the whole world due to their unique carving styles.
pg127_n0014: The sculptures are the attractions for tourists visiting Tanzania.
pg127_n0015: Indeed, there are plenty of Makonde sculptures in museums and various exhibitions worldwide.
pg127_n0016: For instance, China holds the largest collection of Makonde artworks in the world.
pg127_n0017: Due to such popularity, today, Makonde sculpture in Tanzania has attracted artists including the non-Makonde people who are making their living through creating Makonde art.

pg138_n0034: Current situation of art in Tanzania
pg138_n0036: The trends of art in Tanzania were not a limited point of creativity to Tanzanian artists.
pg138_n0037: They were like a road map of cultural entities to grow.
pg138_n0038: During the colonial period, several talented Africans were formally trained to become professional painters and art teachers in various schools in Tanzania and at the Makerere University College in Uganda.
pg138_n0039: Abdullah Farahani, Sam Ntiro, Fatma Abdullah, and professor Elias Jengo, and Raza Mohamed are among a few Tanzanian painters who acquired formal training in visual art.
pg139_n0004: After the independence, the production and promotion of formal visual art such as printmaking, graphics, textiles and fashion design, and animation design flourished in the country.
pg139_n0005: Western cultural patrons recruited formal artist scholars who became ambassadors of the modern art.
pg139_n0007: During independence, most of these artists were involved in various art training programmes, particularly drawing, painting, and printmaking.
pg139_n0008: Since nineteen seventy the Tanzania government established art education at Chang’ombe and Butimba Teachers Colleges, likewise several art projects were implemented at the Nyumba ya Sanaa Art Project and the Tingatinga Arts Society in Dar es Salaam.
pg139_n0009: Other developments include the opening of the Bagamoyo College of Art in nineteen eighty and later on became a Taasisi ya Sanaa na Utamaduni Bagamoyo, TaSUBa, in two thousand and seven, where young talented fine and performing artists were taught.
pg139_n0010: Presently visual art is taught in many primary and secondary schools.
pg139_n0011: The universities of Dar es Salaam and Dodoma have fine art courses which teach art programmes.
pg139_n0013: Some well-known artists are Prof Elias Jengo, Mohamed Raza and Joseph Nyunga.

pg143_n0017: Waste management for social well-being of artist
pg143_n0019: Concept of occupational health and environmental care
pg143_n0021: Occupational health and environmental care are two distinct fields that share a common goal of ensuring the social well-being of the people in the workplace.
pg143_n0022: Both fields are essential in promoting public health by ensuring the safety and prevention of human beings from environmental hazards.
pg143_n0023: The goal is to minimise the impact of waste materials on the environment by reducing the amount of waste generated due to the development of industry, technology and our daily life activities.
pg143_n0027: Waste is a concept that is defined as materials that are unwanted by their producer.
pg143_n0028: These materials have to be managed to make everyone in particular environment
pg144_n0004: Waste management is the process and action that are required to manage waste from the level of its production to its final stage of disposal.
pg144_n0008: Waste management is the practice of using various preventive methods to reduce the negative impact of waste on the environment and human health.
pg144_n0009: The following are the significance of waste management:
pg144_n0011: Preservation of natural resources and reduction of pollution: Appropriate waste management contributes to environmental protection.
pg144_n0013: Public health: By eliminating areas where pests can grow, waste management helps stop the spread of diseases.
pg144_n0015: Sustainability: By decreasing, reusing, and recycling waste, we can protect the environment and reduce the quantity of wastes dumped in landfills.
pg144_n0019: There are many sources which generate waste.
pg144_n0020: Some of them are detailed below:
pg144_n0022: Bulky wastes: There are various sources where waste can be generated.
pg144_n0023: These include shops, offices, hotels, non-government markets, stores, tyres, electronics, plastic bags, bottles, buckets, packaging materials, paper fibres, and discarded electronic waste.
pg144_n0025: Industrial wastes: such as paper and pulp wastes, oil refineries, tanneries, distilleries, thermal power plants, chemical industries, metal smelters, coal, ash, acids, chemicals, textiles, plastics, nuclear wastes, unused metal sheets, metal scraps, rubber, leather, toxic effluents, fibres (residues), heavy metals, solvents, resins, sludge and abrasive.
pg144_n0027: Agricultural wastes: such as farm waste, livestock yards, crop residues, biogases from sugarcane, outdated pesticides and fertilisers, manure, weedicides, fungicides, slaughter waste, plastics and containers.
pg144_n0029: Organics mining wastes: Waste rock, tailings, mine water, chemicals and others.

pg006_n0005_easy_read: This textbook, Fine Art for Secondary Schools, is for Form one students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0006_easy_read:
This book follows the twenty twenty-three Fine Art Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form one to Form four.
The Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, MoEST, issued this syllabus.
pg006_n0007_easy_read:
This book is a revised edition of Fine Art for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form one.
The earlier book was published in twenty twenty-three.
It followed the two thousand and five syllabus issued by the then Ministry of Education and Vocational Training, MoEVT.
pg006_n0009_easy_read:
The book has six chapters:
- Introduction to Fine Art
- Fundamentals of Drawing
- Fundamentals to Painting
- Fundamentals of Printmaking
- Trends of Fine Art in Tanzania
- Occupational Health and Environmental Care
pg006_n0010_easy_read:
Each chapter has:
- text
- activities
- scenarios
- illustrations
- exercises
pg006_n0011_easy_read:
Do all the activities and exercises.
Also do the other assignments your teacher gives you.
pg006_n0012_easy_read:
You must also prepare a portfolio.
Use it to keep records of the activities you do in different lessons.
pg006_n0013_easy_read: This will help you develop the intended competencies.
pg006_n0015_easy_read:
You can find additional learning resources at the T I E e-library:

- o l dot t i e dot g o dot t z
pg007_n0009_easy_read:
Fine art has an important role in daily life.
It affects many parts of our lives in many ways.
pg007_n0010_easy_read:
Some examples of fine art products are:
- images in books
- the emblem on your uniform
- decorations in different places
pg007_n0011_easy_read: Fine art is also an important part of our culture.
pg007_n0012_easy_read: Different societies around the world make and use fine art products for different purposes.
pg007_n0013_easy_read:
These purposes include:
- storytelling
- ceremonial occasions
- prestige
pg007_n0014_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the meaning of fine art
- the principles of fine art
- the elements of fine art
- the relationship between fine art and other subjects
pg007_n0015_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you to understand and value fine art.
Later, they will also help you become an entrepreneur who creates and sells artwork.
pg007_n0018_easy_read: The world without fine art products.
pg007_n0022_easy_read: To understand fine art better, let us first look at the general meaning of art and its different forms.
pg007_n0024_easy_read: Art is a general term for human creativity and imagination that produce different art forms.
pg007_n0025_easy_read:
For many years, people have used different art forms to express:
- feelings
- ideas
- emotions
- thoughts
pg007_n0026_easy_read: Also, people have seen art as the highest form of expression in human life.
pg007_n0027_easy_read:
Artists use different art forms to create works of art.
People use these works of art as another way to communicate messages.
pg007_n0028_easy_read: A form of art includes all the outside, physical features of an artwork.
pg007_n0029_easy_read: A form of art also depends on the size and type of materials or media used to create the artwork.
pg007_n0030_easy_read:
Artists use different art forms to express their imagination.
They also use them to give visual or physical form to their creative ideas.
pg008_n0006_easy_read:
There are three main forms of art:
- visual arts
- literary arts
- performing arts
pg008_n0007_easy_read: The three forms of art are explained below:
pg008_n0011_easy_read: Visual arts are creative works of art that people enjoy by looking at them.
pg008_n0012_easy_read:
Examples of visual arts are:
- drawing
- painting
- sculpture
- printmaking
- design
- craftworks
- photography
- filmmaking
- architecture
pg008_n0013_easy_read: Artists create these works of art to show their ideas and imagination in visual forms.
pg008_n0014_easy_read: Visual arts are important tools for teaching and learning in many ways.
pg008_n0015_easy_read:
Visual arts include:
- illustrations in books
- digital presentations
- other teaching aids, such as spheres, toys, periodicals, and photographs
pg008_n0016_easy_read: Using visual arts skills and knowledge makes learning enjoyable. It helps students connect classroom activities with outdoor activities, such as domestic chores.
pg008_n0020_easy_read: Literary arts are a form of art that people present in spoken or written form.
pg008_n0021_easy_read:
Literary arts include:
- poems
- plays
- stories
- novels
- other creative works that are closely linked to spoken or written communication
pg008_n0022_easy_read:
Works of literary art include:
- magazines
- letters
- manuscripts
- books
pg008_n0023_easy_read:
Literary arts have different genres, such as:
- drama
- poetry
- prose
pg008_n0024_easy_read: Each genre is different in the way it presents messages.
pg008_n0028_easy_read: Performing arts are a form of art where people present different artistic activities on a stage before an audience.
pg008_n0029_easy_read:
These performing arts include:
- acrobatics, performed through body balance
- music, performed through vocals and instruments
- theatre, performed through life experiences
pg008_n0033_easy_read: Fine art means forms of visual art that people mainly create and value for their aesthetic, practical, and intellectual importance.
pg008_n0034_easy_read: Fine art comes from human activities that are part of creative processes.
pg008_n0035_easy_read:
These processes involve:
- preparation
- incubation, or putting together production ideas and materials
- composition of a work of art
- evaluation of the work of art
- production or completion of a work of art
pg009_n0003_easy_read: Fine artists use their creativity, skills and personal views to show their own feelings, ideas and observations about the world, or those of other people.
pg009_n0004_easy_read: Fine art can be a way for artists to express ideas about personal, cultural, social and political issues.
pg009_n0006_easy_read:
People can find fine artworks in many places:
- residential areas
- art shops
- galleries
- public spaces
- museums
- individual collections
- online sources, for example, H T T P S, colon, slash slash, w w w dot artfinder dot com
pg009_n0010_easy_read: Fine art includes many artistic skills. People create and value them for their beauty and their power to express ideas and feelings.
pg009_n0011_easy_read: As technology develops, artists can use different techniques and materials to create visual ideas that people can see and that have a real form.
pg009_n0012_easy_read:
This development has expanded several forms of fine art:
drawing
painting
design
printmaking
sculpture
pg009_n0017_easy_read:
Drawing is the process of making images on a surface with a tool that makes marks, such as:
a pencil
charcoal
a crayon
pg009_n0018_easy_read: Drawing is a basic step in making other forms of fine art, including painting and design.
pg009_n0019_easy_read: A drawing can also be a work of art on its own. It can show a message to an audience.
pg009_n0020_easy_read: Figure one point one shows an example of a drawing of a girl.
pg009_n0022_easy_read: Figure one point one: A drawing of a girl
pg010_n0004_easy_read:
Painting is a type of fine art.
It uses coloured images to show ideas, thoughts, emotions and feelings.
pg010_n0005_easy_read: A painting is a work of art made with paint.
pg010_n0006_easy_read:
People can make a painting on:
walls
paper
canvas
They use brushes and colours.
pg010_n0007_easy_read: Choosing colours well and using them well in a painting creates a skilful and complete picture.
pg010_n0008_easy_read: Also, using colours skilfully adds beauty to paintings and to the places where people display them.
pg010_n0009_easy_read: Figure one point two shows an example of a painting.
pg010_n0011_easy_read: Figure one point two: A painting by Dominicus Makukula
pg010_n0015_easy_read:
Sculpture is a three-dimensional art form.
It involves making physical objects or forms by shaping materials.
pg010_n0016_easy_read: People can make sculptures from many different media or materials.
pg010_n0017_easy_read:
These materials include:
clay
wax
wood
paper
stone
metal
fabric
rubber
glass
gypsum powder
cement
pg010_n0018_easy_read: A sculpture can be figurative or non-figurative.
pg010_n0019_easy_read:
A complete sculpture can be:
in relief
in intaglio
free-standing
sculpture in the round
pg010_n0020_easy_read:
Examples of sculpture works include:
a bust
a statue
a figurine

pg011_n0009_easy_read: Design is another type of art.
pg011_n0010_easy_read: Design is an outline, a sketch, or a visual idea for a work of art that will be made.
pg011_n0011_easy_read:
Works of art like these are products of design:
textile designs
posters
emblems
logos
banners
pg011_n0012_easy_read:
These works first appear as sketches or outlines during the process of making them.
Then they are produced as complete works of art.
pg011_n0013_easy_read:
Design also means the creative activity of planning and organising the elements of art in a work of art.
These elements include:
lines
shapes
colours
textures
space

pg021_n0013_easy_read: Principles of fine art are sometimes called principles of design or principles of art.
pg021_n0014_easy_read: Artists use these guidelines when they arrange parts of an artwork.
pg021_n0015_easy_read: When artists use these principles well, the principles help them make correct actions and decisions in the final artwork.
pg021_n0016_easy_read: Principles of art are guidelines that help artists focus on making a pleasing artwork.
pg021_n0017_easy_read:
These principles include:
- balance
- proportion
- emphasis
- variety
- rhythm
- movement
- harmony
- unity
pg021_n0018_easy_read: The details for each principle are below:
pg021_n0022_easy_read:
The principle of balance means a work has visual equality.
Artists create this by arranging visual elements well, such as line, texture, colour and form.
pg021_n0023_easy_read: When a work of art has balance, it stays stable where it is placed.
pg021_n0024_easy_read:
In design, balance has three types:
- formal balance
- informal balance
- radial balance
pg021_n0025_easy_read: The three types are explained below:
pg021_n0029_easy_read:
Formal balance is also called symmetrical balance.
It means visual equality.
Artists create it by arranging similar or identical elements on both sides of the axis.
pg021_n0030_easy_read: An axis is an imaginary horizontal or vertical line at the centre of a design.
pg021_n0031_easy_read:
Formal balance has two sides in a composition.
The two sides have equal visual weight.
pg021_n0032_easy_read: Figure one point fifteen shows an example of formal balance.
pg021_n0036_easy_read: Figure one point fifteen: Formal balance
pg022_n0006_easy_read: Informal balance is also called asymmetrical balance.
pg022_n0007_easy_read: Informal balance is a way of placing two different objects in a work of art so they have equal visual weight.
pg022_n0008_easy_read: Figure one point sixteen shows an example of informal balance.
pg022_n0010_easy_read: Figure one point sixteen: Informal balance
pg022_n0011_easy_read: Source: Principles of Design: Balance – Terry Grant, raggedclothcafe dot com, two thousand and seven
pg022_n0015_easy_read: Radial balance happens when the parts of a design seem to spread out from the centre of the design.
pg022_n0016_easy_read:
You can see a good example of radial balance in:
- flower petals
- tree rings
- a half-cut orange
- a bicycle wheel

pg023_n0007_easy_read: A well-proportioned artwork shows the right size relationship between the height, width and depth of the design elements.

pg052_n0012_easy_read: Here is safety guidance for handling art materials and equipment:
pg052_n0016_easy_read: Store drawing materials and equipment in a safe place when you are not using them.
pg052_n0019_easy_read: Keep drawing books away from liquid materials so they do not get wet.
pg052_n0022_easy_read: Keep flammable tools away from heat or fire. These include: rubber erasers, plastics, rulers, and oil colours that use turpentine.
pg052_n0025_easy_read: Clean brushes well with the right solvents after each use.
pg052_n0028_easy_read: Do not leave liquid materials open. Examples are: fixative sprays, linseed oils, and solvents. This stops dust from getting into them. This also stops them from drying out in the air.
pg052_n0031_easy_read: Do not fold drawing papers before or after use.
pg052_n0034_easy_read: Do not use sharp tools, such as a razor blade or a knife, to cut anything on the drawing board or table.
pg052_n0035_easy_read: This includes cutting stencils and trimming paper.
pg052_n0036_easy_read: These actions often damage the surface of a drawing board.
pg052_n0039_easy_read: After use, clean erasers with a clean soft cloth. Then put them back in their packet or container.
pg052_n0040_easy_read: This helps keep erasers clean for the next user.
pg052_n0043_easy_read: Do not use pins to fix your paper to the drawing board. Use art clips or art tape instead.
pg052_n0046_easy_read: Keep drawing materials with fluid, such as fountain marker pens, facing down or lying flat to stop leakage.

pg063_n0017_easy_read: A simple decorative drawing is important in our daily life in different ways.
pg063_n0018_easy_read: Some of these are listed below:
pg063_n0020_easy_read: Aesthetic appearance: It adds beauty and makes our surroundings look more attractive.
pg063_n0021_easy_read: It can change ordinary spaces into places that feel welcoming, attractive, and inspiring.
pg063_n0022_easy_read: For example, a well-decorated room can create a positive feeling and improve the user's mood.
pg063_n0024_easy_read: Personal identity: It helps people show their personality, interests, and preferences.
pg063_n0025_easy_read: People can choose colours, patterns, artwork, or objects. Decorations help us create things that show who we are and what we value.
pg063_n0027_easy_read: Creating comfort: It can make a space more comfortable.
pg063_n0028_easy_read: For example, cool colours and warm lighting can make a living room feel more welcoming and comfortable.
pg063_n0030_easy_read: Setting the mood: It can affect our emotions and create the right mood for different occasions.
pg063_n0031_easy_read: For example, festive decorations can create feelings of joy and celebration.
pg064_n0002_easy_read: Social interaction: It can help people meet and spend time together.
pg064_n0003_easy_read: For example, decorated homes or public places can bring people together to talk and share experiences.
pg064_n0005_easy_read: Cultural and historical significance: It can keep cultural and historical importance.
pg064_n0006_easy_read: Traditional ornaments, symbols, or art facts can show personal, social, or national heritage. They can also help keep cultural practices alive.
pg064_n0010_easy_read: An artist needs to follow several steps to make a simple decorative drawing.
pg064_n0011_easy_read: The steps are: concept development, analysis of the idea, planning, and production.
pg064_n0013_easy_read: Concept development: This is the first stage. At this stage, the artist gets the idea for the decorative drawing.
pg064_n0014_easy_read: This stage includes thinking of ideas and imagining what the final piece will look like.
pg064_n0015_easy_read: Artists can get ideas from natural and non-natural sources.
pg064_n0016_easy_read: The place for the decoration also has a big effect on the type of decoration.
pg064_n0017_easy_read: For example, hospitals cannot use animal images as decoration.
pg064_n0019_easy_read: Analysis of idea: At this stage, the artist studies the idea that inspired the drawing to find the most interesting part.
pg064_n0020_easy_read: Then the artist makes preliminary sketches of the decoration images to be drawn.
pg064_n0022_easy_read: Planning: At this stage, the artist decides: the material to use, the equipment to use, the size of the place and the image, the techniques to use, and other needed information, such as the location of the place and other technical details.
pg064_n0023_easy_read: The artist may also make preliminary sketches at this stage.
pg064_n0025_easy_read: Production: This is the final stage. At this stage, the artist draws the decoration by following the prepared plans.

pg069_n0010_easy_read:

pg069_n0011_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you create simple, good-quality paintings by using different techniques.
pg069_n0018_easy_read:
Painting is a form of fine art.
It uses coloured images to express ideas, thoughts, emotions and feelings in a creative way.
pg069_n0019_easy_read: A work of art made by painting is also called a painting.
pg069_n0020_easy_read: People make paintings by using brushes and colours on surfaces such as walls, paper and canvas.
pg069_n0021_easy_read: Painting is one of the oldest and best-known forms of fine art.
pg069_n0022_easy_read: Painting has always been practised together with drawing, design and sculpture.
pg069_n0026_easy_read: In fine art, the materials used to make a painting are called media.
pg069_n0027_easy_read: In painting, the word media or medium means the paints or colours that artists use.
pg069_n0028_easy_read:
Paints are made of three parts:
- pigment
- binder
- solvent
pg069_n0029_easy_read:
Pigment is a fine coloured powder.
It gives paint its colour, or hue.
pg069_n0030_easy_read: Pigment is the main substance in paint.
pg069_n0031_easy_read:
Pigment is made from:
- animal remains
- plants
- rocks
- minerals
- soils

pg070_n0006_easy_read: It is a liquid that dry pigment is added to.
pg070_n0007_easy_read: The binder makes the pigment thick.
pg070_n0008_easy_read: In painting, linseed oil is used to make paint more liquid and glossy.
pg070_n0009_easy_read: A solvent is a liquid used to dissolve paint.
pg070_n0010_easy_read:
For example:
- Turpentine is a solvent for oil paints.
- Linseed oil is a solvent for oil paints.
- Kerosene is a solvent for oil paints.
- Water is a solvent for watercolours.
pg070_n0011_easy_read: Solvents are also used to clean brushes.
pg070_n0012_easy_read:
Paint is the main material used for painting.
It comes in different forms:
- tubes
- tins
- powder
- plastic containers
pg070_n0013_easy_read: Paints are grouped by the type of solvent they use.
pg070_n0014_easy_read:
These include:
- oil paints
- watercolours
- acrylics
- gouache
- tempera
pg070_n0016_easy_read: Oil paint: This is paint made with oil.
pg070_n0017_easy_read:
Oil paint was first used in the fourteen hundreds.
It is still one of the most popular painting media in the world.
pg070_n0019_easy_read: Watercolour: This is a painting medium in which the pigment is mixed with water.
pg070_n0020_easy_read: Watercolour is the most sensitive painting medium because it dries quickly.
pg070_n0021_easy_read:
Watercolour also reacts to the lightest touch of the artist.
It can become spoiled very quickly if it is not used carefully.
pg070_n0023_easy_read:
Acrylic: This is a water-based synthetic paint that dries quickly.
It is a manufactured paint with plastic binders.
pg070_n0024_easy_read:
Acrylic is very flexible to use.
It can be applied in thick layers and thin glaze.
pg070_n0025_easy_read: When acrylic is dry, it resists water.
pg070_n0027_easy_read:
Gouache is an opaque watercolour medium.
It is made from natural pigment with gum Arabic or dextrin binder.
pg070_n0028_easy_read:
Gouache can be used to make different kinds of artwork, including:
- murals
- illustrations
- comics
pg070_n0030_easy_read: Tempera: This is a painting medium in which the pigment is mixed with egg yolk and water.
pg070_n0031_easy_read:
Tempera is a very old painting medium.
People have used it for thousands of years.
pg070_n0032_easy_read: For example, in the early Christian art era, artists used tempera a lot to paint images of religious icons.
pg070_n0036_easy_read: Painting equipment means the tools or instruments used for painting.
pg070_n0039_easy_read:
Painting brushes: These brushes are used to put paint or colour onto the surface of:
- paper
- board
- canvas
pg070_n0040_easy_read: Brushes come in different sizes and shapes.
pg070_n0041_easy_read:
The shape and size of a brush are important.
Each brush is made for a particular type and size of colour stroke.
pg070_n0042_easy_read: The size of a brush depends on the type, shape, and size of its bristles.
pg070_n0043_easy_read: There are special brushes for different paints or media.
pg070_n0044_easy_read: Sable brushes are the most common brushes used by artists.
pg070_n0045_easy_read:
They are common because they work well with different colours, such as:
- tempera
- oil colours
- acrylics
- watercolours
They do not break or wear down easily.

pg071_n0007_easy_read: Watercolour papers: These papers are made to use with water-based paints.
pg071_n0008_easy_read: Watercolour papers absorb water. You can apply colours many times without the paper losing its shape.
pg071_n0010_easy_read: Some watercolour papers are smooth. Other watercolour papers are rough.
pg071_n0012_easy_read: Palette: An artist uses this tool to hold and mix colours before painting.
pg071_n0013_easy_read: Most palettes are made from plastic, wood, or aluminium.
pg071_n0014_easy_read: Palettes resist water. This makes paint easy to remove. It also helps the artist mix colours well.

- drying brushes
- wiping painting surfaces
- cleaning up spills
- drying hands

pg072_n0006_easy_read: Handle painting materials and equipment properly for safety.
pg072_n0007_easy_read: Follow several rules wherever painting materials and equipment are used.
pg072_n0008_easy_read: Follow these general rules and procedures to keep materials, equipment, and the user or artist safe:
pg072_n0012_easy_read: Artists should read the user guides on labels of art materials and equipment carefully before they use them for the first time.
pg072_n0015_easy_read: Follow all warnings and precautions on the labels of painting materials and equipment carefully.
pg072_n0018_easy_read: Keep paint containers and tubes tightly closed when you are not using them.
pg072_n0021_easy_read: All material containers must have labels.
pg072_n0022_easy_read: For example, label solvent containers to avoid confusion when using them.
pg072_n0023_easy_read: If the water container does not have a label, people can easily confuse it with other odourless and colourless solvents.
pg072_n0026_easy_read:
Clean and dry brushes and other art equipment properly after use.
Keep them in their cases.
Do not leave them with paint on them or soaking in a solvent container.
pg072_n0027_easy_read:
This helps to:
- keep the equipment in good condition
- make the equipment last longer
pg072_n0028_easy_read:
This prevents:
- a build-up of paint, ink, or other materials that can damage the equipment over time
- contamination of the materials used in the artwork

pg073_n0025_easy_read: When light shines on objects, things and living organisms, we see colours on them.
pg073_n0026_easy_read: So, colour is what we see on objects or things in light.
pg073_n0027_easy_read: When you mix, match, compare or contrast colours, you use science.
pg073_n0028_easy_read: When you use colours in a creative way to communicate or express ideas, thoughts and feelings, you create art.
pg073_n0032_easy_read: Artists use different ways and techniques of painting to get the qualities they want in their work.
pg073_n0033_easy_read: A good understanding of types of colours and their basic properties helps artists use colour well in painting and get the results they want.
pg073_n0034_easy_read: This part explains three main properties of colours.
pg073_n0035_easy_read: These properties are hue, value and intensity.
pg073_n0038_easy_read: Hue means colour in its original form.
pg073_n0039_easy_read: Hue is a special property or feature of a certain colour quality.
pg073_n0040_easy_read: For example, blue, red and yellow are attributes of colour.
pg073_n0043_easy_read: Value is the lightness or darkness of a colour.
pg073_n0044_easy_read: When working with hues, you can change value by adding black or white.
pg073_n0045_easy_read: Adding black medium to a hue makes the value darker. This is called a shade in colour.
pg073_n0046_easy_read: In the same way, adding white medium to a colour makes the value lighter or whiter. This is called a tint.
pg073_n0049_easy_read: Intensity is the brightness or dullness of a colour.
pg073_n0050_easy_read: The intensity of a colour is also called Chroma or Saturation.
pg073_n0051_easy_read: The intensity of colour is a
pg074_n0004_easy_read: This is the result of tinting or shading.
pg074_n0005_easy_read: These processes happen when colours are put on a painting.
pg074_n0006_easy_read:
A bright colour has high intensity.
A dull colour has low intensity.
pg074_n0008_easy_read:
Note:
People may use the words intensity and value in the same way, but they do not mean the same thing.
pg074_n0009_easy_read:
The difference is this:
- Value changes when you add black or white to a hue.
- Intensity changes when you mix a colour with its complementary colour on the colour wheel or with grey.
pg074_n0013_easy_read:
A colour wheel is a circle of colours.
It shows how colours are related to each other.
pg074_n0014_easy_read: A colour wheel helps people understand where different colours come from.
pg074_n0015_easy_read:
On the colour wheel, some colours are natural.
Other colours are made by mixing two or more natural colours.
pg074_n0019_easy_read: There are three groups of colours, based on how they are formed or where they come from.
pg074_n0020_easy_read:
These groups are:
- primary colours
- secondary colours
- tertiary or intermediate colours
pg074_n0023_easy_read: Red, yellow and blue are primary colours, also called hues.
pg074_n0024_easy_read: These colours are placed equally around the colour wheel.
pg074_n0025_easy_read: Primary colours come from nature, such as minerals and plants.
pg074_n0026_easy_read: You can mix these colours in different amounts to make all other colours.
pg074_n0027_easy_read: However, you cannot make these colours by mixing other colours.

pg075_n0006_easy_read: Secondary colours are usually placed between the primary colours on a colour wheel.

pg076_n0002_easy_read: Tertiary or intermediate colours are colours you make by mixing a primary colour with the secondary colour next to it.
pg076_n0003_easy_read: Tertiary colours made in this process include: blue-green, blue-purple, red-purple, red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green.
pg076_n0004_easy_read: Figure three point seven shows how tertiary colours are formed.

pg077_n0013_easy_read: A colour scheme is the arrangement or combination of colours and how they affect visibility.
pg077_n0014_easy_read: People use colour schemes to make something look different and more visually attractive.
pg077_n0015_easy_read: The main colour schemes are: monochromatic, analogous, complementary, cool colours, warm colours.
pg077_n0018_easy_read: Analogous colours are colours placed side by side with primary colours on a colour wheel.
pg077_n0019_easy_read: For example, these colours are analogous colours: violet, red, red violet, red-orange. They share the same red base hue.
pg077_n0022_easy_read: Warm colours are colours that give a warm feeling.
pg077_n0023_easy_read: These colours include: red, yellow, orange.
pg077_n0024_easy_read: Cool colours, such as green, blue and purple, create a calm and cold feeling.
pg077_n0025_easy_read: People usually use cool colours in art to create relaxed or calm feelings.
pg077_n0026_easy_read: Figure three point nine shows warm and cool colours.
pg077_n0029_easy_read: Complementary colours are colours that are opposite each other on the colour wheel.
pg077_n0030_easy_read: These pairs are complementary colours: yellow and purple, orange and blue, yellow-green and red-purple, red and green.

pg078_n0012_easy_read: The word monochrome comes from Greek.

pg079_n0026_easy_read: There are several types of watercolour paint that an artist can use.
pg079_n0027_easy_read: These types include: tube watercolours, liquid watercolours, and dry cake or pan watercolours.
pg079_n0028_easy_read: Tube watercolours are paints in metal or plastic tubes. Liquid watercolours are pigments mixed in a water-based solution and stored in tins or cans.
pg079_n0029_easy_read: Dry cake or pan watercolours come as dry cakes in small plastic pans. They need more water to make them ready for painting.
pg079_n0030_easy_read: Other watercolours come as coloured pencils and crayons.
pg079_n0031_easy_read: Water-soluble coloured pencils give a different effect when you use them dry.
pg079_n0035_easy_read: Painting with watercolours is very challenging because it dries very fast. This makes mixing layers difficult.
pg079_n0036_easy_read: Watercolour layers also spread easily. This makes the edges hard to control.
pg079_n0037_easy_read: A person needs a lot of practice to master watercolour painting techniques.
pg079_n0038_easy_read: Painting techniques such as wet-on-dry, wet-on-wet, wash and dry-on-dry need a lot of practice before use in actual painting.
pg079_n0041_easy_read: Wet-on-dry is a technique where you use a wet paintbrush on dry paper.
pg079_n0042_easy_read: Wet-on-dry is suitable for adding details and giving the painting sharp, clean edges.
pg079_n0045_easy_read: Wet-on-wet is a technique that is almost like wet-on-dry. In wet-on-wet, you apply paint on wet paper instead of dry paper.
pg079_n0046_easy_read: People often use this technique in painting to blend colours.
pg080_n0005_easy_read: Wash technique: This technique means putting paint evenly on dry or wet paper.
pg080_n0006_easy_read: Artists use wash to make a background in a painting and to show even colour.
pg080_n0007_easy_read: You can practise this technique with one colour or more colours.
pg080_n0009_easy_read: Dry-on-dry technique: In this technique, you use a dry brush with very little paint. You move it lightly and quickly across dry paper.
pg080_n0010_easy_read: This technique is good for adding details to a painting. For example: fur on a dog, leaves on a tree, and long hair on a girl’s head.
pg080_n0014_easy_read: Colours have several uses in art.
pg080_n0015_easy_read: Artists use colours to: decorate places, communicate messages, and improve works of art.
pg080_n0016_easy_read: These are the common uses of colour in art:
pg080_n0020_easy_read: Colours help us recognise objects and see them more clearly. We recognise objects more quickly when their colours match what we see in real life.
pg080_n0023_easy_read: Colours can symbolise something with cultural value.
pg080_n0026_easy_read: Colours can show emotions and feelings.
pg080_n0027_easy_read: Artists use colours to communicate their thoughts, ideas and feelings.
pg080_n0028_easy_read: For example, warm colours such as red, orange and yellow can show warmth, passion and energy. Cool colours such as blue, green and purple can show calmness, peace and relaxation.
pg080_n0029_easy_read: Also, an artist can use colours to show their feelings or to communicate wider social and cultural ideas that people connect with certain colours.
pg080_n0032_easy_read: Colours can influence or guide how the audience appreciates a work of art.
pg080_n0035_easy_read: Colours are used to emphasise some parts of a work of art and to attract viewers' attention to the artist’s work.

pg081_n0018_easy_read: Artists get the subject of their paintings from: memory, imagination, and observation.
pg081_n0019_easy_read: When an artist chooses the source of the artwork, the artist makes sketches of ideas, thoughts, feelings, or imagination. The artist also prepares all the tools and equipment needed for the work.
pg081_n0020_easy_read: In the same way, the artist also prepares when painting from direct observation of nature or experience.
pg081_n0022_easy_read: Painting from memory: This is a way of painting where the artist shows parts of images of a subject remembered from past experiences.
pg081_n0023_easy_read: When an artist paints from memory, it is very difficult to compare the original subject with the finished artwork.
pg081_n0025_easy_read: Painting from imagination: This is a little different from painting from memory. In the final artwork, the artist creates something that is not a representation of anything that existed before.
pg081_n0026_easy_read: Imaginative painting uses: images, shapes, and colour schemes. These are created from scratch, based on ideas the artist sees in the mind.
pg081_n0028_easy_read: Painting from observation: Artists use this approach when they want to paint a subject or object correctly, but not exactly.
pg081_n0029_easy_read: Artists also use this approach in other types of painting, such as still-life painting.
pg081_n0030_easy_read: It involves looking at different subjects, such as: landscapes, seascapes, animals, plants, and still-life set-ups.
pg081_n0031_easy_read: The difference between painting from observation and still-life painting is that still-life painting has representational features that are not needed in painting from observation.
pg081_n0033_easy_read: Still-life painting: This is a style of painting that uses arranged non-living objects placed on a flat surface or a table.
pg081_n0034_easy_read: The artist should produce an exact copy of the objects shown in the painting.

pg083_n0008_easy_read: Simple decorative painting means simple paint designs that an artist can put on many surfaces to decorate them, such as: a wall, an object, a picture frame, furniture, canvas, a roof, fabric, and paper.
pg083_n0012_easy_read: Each decorative painting has its own benefits.
pg083_n0013_easy_read: Some decorative paintings can be used outside and inside.
pg083_n0014_easy_read: Other decorative paintings can create metallic or rust finishes. The rest are waterproof.
pg083_n0015_easy_read: For this reason, it is necessary to check the needs of each coating before you use it.
pg083_n0016_easy_read: In general, decorative painting is used to change how a surface looks.
pg083_n0017_easy_read: Its main purpose is to make the original surface look more beautiful.

pg096_n0009_easy_read: Printmaking is an important part of our life.
pg096_n0010_easy_read:
Printmaking is very useful in daily life.
It lets people make copies of images and texts.
pg096_n0011_easy_read: Printmaking is in every part of our life.
pg096_n0012_easy_read:
Many things we use come from printmaking.
These include:
- the clothes we wear
- our books
- business adverts on streets, such as posters and billboards
pg096_n0013_easy_read: Printmaking helps us feel comfortable and enjoy life.
pg096_n0014_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about printmaking.
You will learn about:
- its meaning
- its techniques
- its materials
- its tools and equipment
- how to create simple decorative monoprints
pg096_n0015_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you create and produce simple prints.
These skills can help you become an entrepreneur in printmaking activities.

pg096_n0022_easy_read:
Printmaking is an art process.
It means moving images from a matrix to another surface, usually paper or fabric.
pg096_n0023_easy_read:
A print is an artwork made with ink on a flat surface.
For example:
- canvas
- paper
- fabric
- cups
pg096_n0024_easy_read:
The plate is the place where you put and create the original image.
You use it to print many copies.
pg096_n0025_easy_read:
This process does not use painting or drawing on a surface.
Instead, you press paper onto the inked image surface.
pg096_n0026_easy_read: Printmaking helps artists make more copies of the original artwork in a short time.
pg096_n0027_easy_read: For example, an artist can print five hundred T-shirts for a campaign in one day by using printmaking.
pg096_n0028_easy_read: This task could take longer if the artist used other methods, such as painting or drawing.
pg096_n0029_easy_read:
Printmaking is also used for:
- making rubber stamps
- printing on difficult areas, such as very high walls
- decorating fabrics, such as table covers, curtains and bed sheets
pg096_n0030_easy_read: Printmaking is done in different ways and with different techniques.
pg097_n0006_easy_read: Printmaking can be done in different ways.
pg097_n0007_easy_read: Some of these techniques are stencil, relief, intaglio and screen printing.
pg097_n0011_easy_read: A stencil uses a thin sheet of hard paper or plastic. You cut a design into it and then print it.
pg097_n0012_easy_read: A stencil can be used to make the cut design on the surface where you place it.
pg097_n0013_easy_read: You do this process by putting ink or paint on the stencil. You can use spray paint. You can also use thick paint with a sponge or a brush.
pg097_n0014_easy_read: Then the pigment goes through the holes in the stencil. This makes pattern shapes appear in the design.
pg097_n0015_easy_read: Figure four point one shows a prepared stencil. Figure four point two, a, and Figure four point two, b, show the stencil printing process.
pg097_n0019_easy_read: The materials, tools and equipment used for stencil printing are:
pg097_n0021_easy_read: Stencil film: This is hard paper or plastic used to make a stencil.
pg097_n0022_easy_read: The cut design is placed on the stencil film.
pg097_n0024_easy_read: Carving knife: This is a flat, sharp-edged metal tool used to cut the design out of a stencil film.
pg097_n0026_easy_read: Masking tape: This is thin paper tape used to stick stencils and the paper for printing together.
pg097_n0028_easy_read: Printing ink: This is a liquid or paste used for printing on a surface.
pg097_n0029_easy_read: When printing ink is used, it leaves a particular mark on a design.
pg097_n0031_easy_read: Squeegee: This is a tool used to spread ink evenly on the stencil.
pg097_n0033_easy_read: Printing papers: These are special printmaking papers used for relief printing.
pg097_n0034_easy_read: Printing papers are chosen because they hold ink well and make high-quality prints.
pg097_n0035_easy_read: The thickness and texture of the paper can change the final look of the print.
pg097_n0037_easy_read: Printing table: A flat and stable surface for putting on ink and for stencil printing.

pg097_n0043_easy_read: Design creation: Finish the design by using the sketch as a guide and making improvements. This can be done on a computer using design software.

pg100_n0010_easy_read: However, artists can also use other materials that are easy to get.

Relief printing has several steps:
- create an image for printing
- transfer the image
- cut the plate to show the image to be printed
pg100_n0013_easy_read: First, the artist draws the image on a flat plate.
pg100_n0014_easy_read:
In relief printing, the printing plate is made by removing the parts that will not be printed.
In other words, the background is removed so it stays white when printing.
pg100_n0015_easy_read: The parts left on the original surface receive the ink.
pg100_n0016_easy_read: In this printing process, the parts you do not want to print are cut away.
pg100_n0017_easy_read: The raised parts that are left are inked and printed.
pg100_n0018_easy_read: Relief printing can be done by hand or with a printing press.
pg100_n0022_easy_read: Various materials are used in relief printing:
pg100_n0025_easy_read: This is sometimes called a printing block.
pg100_n0026_easy_read: It is the most important material in relief printing.
pg100_n0027_easy_read: It can be made from different materials, including:
pg100_n0030_easy_read:
Woodblocks are often used.
Different materials can be chosen for the result you want, such as:
- linoleum
- plywood
- hardwood
pg100_n0033_easy_read:
Linoleum blocks are also called lino-cut.
They are softer and easier to carve than woodblocks.
This makes them popular with beginners and artists who want a quicker process.
pg100_n0036_easy_read: Rubber blocks, or soft sculpture blocks, give a flexible surface that is easy to carve.
pg100_n0038_easy_read:
Artists can also use other materials, such as:
- potatoes
- cassava
- linoleum
pg100_n0041_easy_read: Relief printmakers use different tools to carve the block and make the image.
pg100_n0042_easy_read:
Some of these tools are:
- carving knives
- chisels
- trimming knives
- sandpapers
- razorblades
- other related carving tools
pg101_n0006_easy_read:
Printing ink:
Printing ink for relief printing is usually oil-based or water-based.
It comes in different colours.
pg101_n0007_easy_read:
Oil-based inks are more traditional.
They take longer to dry.
People often use them when printing on paper.
pg101_n0008_easy_read:
Water-based inks are better for beginners.
They are easier to clean up.
They dry faster.
pg101_n0010_easy_read:
Printing paper:
Special printmaking paper is used for relief printing.
pg101_n0011_easy_read:
Printmaking papers are chosen because they hold ink well.
They also make high-quality prints.
pg101_n0012_easy_read: The thickness and texture of the paper can change the final look of the print.
pg101_n0016_easy_read: Relief printing often uses many of the same tools and materials as other printing methods.
pg101_n0017_easy_read: Here are some of these tools and materials:
pg101_n0019_easy_read:
Brayer:
A brayer is also called an ink roller.
It is used to spread ink evenly on the surface of the block.
pg101_n0020_easy_read:
The brayer spreads the ink smoothly.
This helps to make prints that are even and clean.
pg101_n0022_easy_read:
Printing press:
A printing press can give even pressure.
This helps to make more even prints, especially for large editions.
pg101_n0024_easy_read:
Printing table:
This is a flat and stable surface for inking and printing the blocks.
pg101_n0026_easy_read:
Baren:
A baren is a hand-held tool.
It is used to apply pressure when making relief prints by hand.
It is especially useful for small-scale works.
pg101_n0028_easy_read:
Protective gear:
Relief printmaking can involve sharp tools.
So it is recommended to wear gloves and eye protection to stay safe during carving.
pg101_n0032_easy_read: These are the steps in relief printing:
pg101_n0034_easy_read:
Design creation:
Use sketch paper to draw a design from a given theme.
The art teacher can choose an attractive theme for you.

For example, the design can be:

- a flower
- an animal

pg101_n0037_easy_read:
Transfer the completed drawn image:
There are several ways to transfer an image from a sketchbook to a relief printmaking plate.

pg103_n0026_easy_read: Intaglio printing is a traditional printing method. People use it to make high-quality images or designs on: paper, currency, postage stamps, and other valuable documents.
pg103_n0027_easy_read: The word "intaglio" comes from an Italian word. It means "engraved" or "cut in". This meaning describes the main feature of this printing method.
pg103_n0028_easy_read: The intaglio printing process can produce: fine details, rich tones, and high-quality prints. This makes it very suitable for printing: banknotes, security documents, and valuable art prints.
pg103_n0029_easy_read: Intaglio printing is complex and needs skilled work. This also makes it hard to copy.
pg103_n0030_easy_read: This has helped people use intaglio printing to prevent copying of currency and other important documents.

pg104_n0009_easy_read: Intaglio printing needs specific materials, tools, and equipment. These are used to make the engraved plates and the final prints.
pg104_n0010_easy_read: The main items used in intaglio printing are:
pg104_n0012_easy_read: Metal plates: copper plates, zinc plates, and steel plates. These plates are often used as the base material for intaglio printing.
pg104_n0013_easy_read: Copper is the most traditional choice. It is easy to shape and it holds ink very well.
pg104_n0015_easy_read: Printing ink: Specialised intaglio printing inks are used.
pg104_n0016_easy_read: These inks are usually oil-based. They are thicker, so they stick well to the engraved lines and grooves on the plate.
pg104_n0018_easy_read: Printing paper: High-quality, damp paper is used for printing.
pg104_n0019_easy_read: The paper must be able to take the pressure used in printing. It must also absorb the ink from the plate well.
pg104_n0023_easy_read: The following tools and equipment are used in an intaglio printing press:
pg105_n0005_easy_read: Etching needle: An etching needle is a pointed tool. People use it to make fine lines and small details on the metal plate during engraving.
pg105_n0007_easy_read: Burin: A burin is a special engraving tool with a sharp tip shaped like a V.
pg105_n0008_easy_read: A burin is used to cut wider lines. It also removes metal from the plate to make shaded areas.
pg105_n0010_easy_read: Roulette: This is a small tool shaped like a spiked wheel. People use it to make a random texture or pattern on the plate.
pg105_n0011_easy_read: People often use this technique for backgrounds or areas that need shading.
pg105_n0013_easy_read: Scraper slash burnisher: The scraper removes extra ink from the plate during wiping. The burnisher smooths and polishes the surface of the plate before printing.
pg105_n0015_easy_read: Intaglio printing press: This is a strong printing press made especially for intaglio printing.
pg105_n0016_easy_read: The press uses strong pressure to move the ink from the engraved plate to the paper.
pg105_n0018_easy_read: Wiping cloth slash pads: These cloths or pads wipe extra ink from the plate. They leave ink only in the engraved lines and grooves.
pg105_n0020_easy_read: Dampening system: This is a system that moistens the printing paper. It keeps the paper damp during printing.
pg105_n0021_easy_read: This helps the paper pick up the ink from the plate more easily.
pg105_n0023_easy_read: Drying racks: These are used to lay out and dry freshly printed sheets of paper.
pg105_n0027_easy_read: The intaglio printing process has these steps:
pg105_n0029_easy_read: Plate preparation: A metal plate is prepared for engraving. The plate is usually made of: copper, zinc, and steel.
pg105_n0030_easy_read: The surface of the plate is polished and cleaned. This makes the base smooth and even.
pg105_n0032_easy_read: Engraving: Skilled workers, called engravers or etchers, use special tools to cut the image into the surface of the plate.
pg105_n0033_easy_read: This process makes fine lines and different depths. These show different tones and shades in the final print.
pg105_n0034_easy_read: The engraved plate becomes the main image that will be transferred onto the paper.
pg106_n0002_easy_read: Inking: Put ink on the whole surface of the engraved plate.
pg106_n0003_easy_read: After inking, the plate is wiped clean. The ink stays only in the cut lines and grooves.
pg106_n0005_easy_read: Wiping: Carefully wipe the surface of the plate to remove extra ink. The ink stays only in the engraved areas.
pg106_n0007_easy_read: Printing: Put a damp sheet of high-quality paper on the inked plate. Then apply pressure to transfer the ink from the plate to the paper.
pg106_n0008_easy_read: People usually apply this pressure with: a roller press; an intaglio printing press. This pushes the paper into the cut lines so the paper picks up the ink.
pg106_n0009_easy_read: This gives the final print a high level of detail and depth.
pg106_n0011_easy_read: Drying: Leave the printed paper to dry fully before any more processing or handling.
pg106_n0014_easy_read: Design and make a copper plate of your choice using engraving and etching techniques.
pg106_n0015_easy_read: Then make prints on paper using your copper plate designs.
pg106_n0019_easy_read: This is a method for transferring a motif or design by using a screen.
pg106_n0020_easy_read: A special mesh is fixed to the frame and stretched tightly over it.
pg106_n0021_easy_read: Then the image is transferred to the screen. Lastly, the squeegee pushes the ink. This helps the paint pass through the transparent motif on the screen to the surface.
pg106_n0022_easy_read: Screen printing is widely used for many things, including: t-shirts; posters; signage; textiles; electronics; more.
pg106_n0023_easy_read: Screen printing can print on different surfaces. The prints also have bright colours and last well. This makes screen printing a popular choice for many printing projects.

pg107_n0009_easy_read: Screen printing needs specific tools and materials. These tools and materials make the stencils and put ink onto the printing surface.
pg107_n0010_easy_read: These are the main tools and materials used in screen printing:
pg107_n0012_easy_read: Screen: The screen is the most important tool in screen printing.
pg107_n0013_easy_read: The screen is usually made of a frame and a tightly stretched mesh.
pg107_n0014_easy_read: The mesh material can be different, for example polyester or nylon. The choice depends on the printing job and the type of ink.
pg107_n0016_easy_read: Squeegee: A squeegee is a hand-held tool. It has a rubber or polyurethane blade. It pushes ink through the open parts of the screen and onto the printing surface.
pg107_n0018_easy_read: Printing press: A screen printing press holds the screen firmly in place. It allows accurate and consistent printing.
pg107_n0019_easy_read: There are different types of presses, including manual and automatic presses.
pg107_n0021_easy_read: Exposure unit: An exposure unit exposes the screen to U V light after the design has been put onto the emulsion.
pg107_n0022_easy_read: This makes the emulsion hard in the areas that the design does not block. As a result, the stencil is made.
pg107_n0024_easy_read: Washout booth or sink: After exposure, the screen must be washed to remove the unhardened emulsion.
pg107_n0025_easy_read: A washout booth or sink is used for this. It has water and may also have a pressure washer.
pg107_n0027_easy_read: Drying racks: Drying racks store and dry freshly printed materials without smudging the ink.
pg108_n0007_easy_read: These are the materials used in screen printing:
pg108_n0009_easy_read: Screen mesh: The mesh comes in different thread counts, or mesh counts, per inch. This affects how much detail the print can show.
pg108_n0010_easy_read: Choose the mesh count based on: how complex the artwork is; the type of ink you are using.
pg108_n0012_easy_read: Emulsion: Emulsion is a liquid that reacts to light. You put it on the screen mesh.
pg108_n0013_easy_read: The emulsion becomes solid when U V light hits it. This creates the stencil.
pg108_n0015_easy_read: Transparent film or vellum: The design is printed on transparent film or vellum. This is used to transfer the artwork onto the screen covered with emulsion during exposure.
pg108_n0017_easy_read: Screen printing ink: Screen printing ink comes in different types: water-based ink; plastisol ink; discharge ink.
pg108_n0018_easy_read: The choice of ink depends on: the printing surface, for example fabric or paper; the effect you want, for example opaque, soft, or vibrant colours.
pg108_n0020_easy_read: Substrate: The material you print on is called the substrate. It can be: fabric; paper; glass; metal; plastic.
pg108_n0022_easy_read: Clean-up supplies: Chemicals and solvents are used for: cleaning the screen; removing extra ink; reclaiming screens so you can use them again.
pg108_n0024_easy_read: Registration guides: These guides help line up the different colour layers during multicolour printing. This helps the final design look sharp and clear.
pg108_n0026_easy_read: Note: A motif used in the screen method should be printed with thick, good-quality ink.
pg108_n0027_easy_read: Kerosene or any cooking oil must be available. It helps moisten a screen motif on paper. This makes it easier to transfer the motif from the paper to the screen.
pg108_n0028_easy_read: The mixing ratio for photo emulsion is partly an estimate. A simple estimate is this: Mix one teaspoon of sensitiser in five hundred millilitres of water. Shake it well so the sensitiser dissolves in the water.
pg108_n0029_easy_read: Then take five teaspoons of photo emulsion and two teaspoons of sensitizer.
pg109_n0008_easy_read: These are the steps for making a mesh screen:
pg109_n0012_easy_read: Make a frame from pieces of wood. Then fix the mesh onto the frame.
pg109_n0015_easy_read: Mix photo emulsion with a small amount of sensitiser. Then stir the mixture.
pg109_n0016_easy_read: Do this in a dark place.
pg109_n0019_easy_read: Use a squeegee to pick up the photo emulsion. Then put it on the mesh screen in a dark room.
pg109_n0022_easy_read: Dry the mesh screen with a heat gun, drier or fan. Then leave it for a short time so the screen can dry.
pg109_n0025_easy_read: Take a motif printed on paper and attach it to the back of the mesh screen.
pg109_n0026_easy_read: The motif should face the mesh screen.
pg109_n0027_easy_read: The image of the motif should touch the mesh screen. Then pour kerosene on the paper motif in a dark place.
pg109_n0030_easy_read: Place a transparent mirror on the screen mesh, behind the paper motif. Then tighten the mirror, the paper motif and the screen mesh together.
pg109_n0033_easy_read: Put the mesh, the motif and the mirror under the needed light.
pg109_n0034_easy_read: Remember, the transparent mirror should face the light for 2 minutes to 10 minutes.
pg109_n0035_easy_read: This depends on the amount of light and the photo emulsion mixture.
pg109_n0038_easy_read: Remove the mirror and the motif paper from the screen. Then clean the screen slowly with a sponge and water.
pg109_n0039_easy_read: When a motif appears on the screen, use the spray gun to wash the screen until the motif can be seen clearly.
pg109_n0042_easy_read: Dry the screen with a heat gun or in sunlight.
pg109_n0044_easy_read: Note: if the motif does not appear on the screen mesh, there may be too much sensitiser in the photo emulsion, or the screen may not have been exposed to light for long enough.
pg109_n0045_easy_read: To solve this problem, either add a sensitiser to the photo emulsion or increase the time of exposure to light rays.
pg109_n0049_easy_read: The steps for making the printing screen are explained above. Now the printing process can be done without any problem.
pg109_n0050_easy_read: Look at the following steps for using the finished screen to print on a chosen surface.
pg110_n0005_easy_read: Setup and registration: Put the screen onto the screen-printing press. The press holds the screen firmly in place.
pg110_n0006_easy_read: Proper registration is very important. It makes sure each colour layer lines up exactly with the others in the final print.
pg110_n0008_easy_read: Ink application: Put the correct ink on its matching screen.
pg110_n0009_easy_read: A squeegee spreads the ink over the open parts of the screen. It pushes the ink through the mesh and onto the printing surface.
pg110_n0011_easy_read: Printing process: The printer pulls the squeegee across the screen. This pushes the ink through the mesh and onto the material.
pg110_n0012_easy_read: Repeat this process for each colour layer. This lets the ink overlap and make the full-colour design.
pg110_n0014_easy_read: Curing: When printing is finished, the printed material usually goes through a curing unit or oven.
pg110_n0015_easy_read: This process cures the ink. It makes the ink stronger and more resistant to fading or washing out.
pg110_n0017_easy_read: Clean-up: After printing, clean the screen very well. Remove any ink and emulsion left on it. This lets you use the screen again for future printing work.
pg110_n0019_easy_read: Prepare your design: Create or choose a design for your screen printing.
pg110_n0020_easy_read: You can draw the design straight onto a piece of paper. Or you can print the design from a computer.
pg110_n0021_easy_read: If you are a beginner, simple designs with bold lines work best.
pg110_n0023_easy_read: Set up your printing area: Put down old newspapers or cardboard. This protects your work surface from ink spills.
pg110_n0025_easy_read: Apply ink to the screen: Put your mesh screen over the printing area with the mesh side facing down.
pg110_n0026_easy_read: Pour a small amount of ink along the top edge of the screen.
pg110_n0028_easy_read: Spread the ink: Use the squeegee to spread the ink evenly over the design area. Press gently.
pg110_n0029_easy_read: Make sure a thin layer of ink covers the whole design.
pg110_n0031_easy_read: Print your design: Carefully lift the mesh screen off the printing surface. This shows your printed design.
pg110_n0032_easy_read: Let the print dry completely before you start the next print.
pg110_n0034_easy_read: Clean the screen: After printing, clean the ink off the mesh screen with water and a gentle brush.
pg110_n0035_easy_read: Make sure the screen is completely dry before you store it for future use.

pg111_n0010_easy_read: This printmaking method makes simple and unique images. Each image is a one-of-a-kind decoration.
pg111_n0011_easy_read: This method means making an image on a flat surface, such as a plate or a piece of glass. Then you transfer the image to paper or another surface with ink.
pg111_n0012_easy_read: Traditional printmaking can make many prints from one plate. Monoprints are different. A monoprint is usually a one-of-a-kind print. This is why the name "mono" means a single printing.
pg111_n0013_easy_read: This process lets you experiment. It also gives you many ways to express your art.
pg111_n0014_easy_read: Here is an overview of monoprinting techniques.
pg111_n0018_easy_read: Some materials are necessary for monoprinting.
pg111_n0021_easy_read: Printing plate: A flat surface where the image is made.
pg111_n0022_easy_read:
The printing plate can be made from:
- plexiglas
- metal
- glass
- a smooth surface that does not absorb liquid, such as acrylic
pg111_n0024_easy_read:
Printing ink or paint: Artists can use printing inks made for printmaking.
They can also use different types of paint that suit the chosen technique, for example acrylics for direct painting.
pg111_n0026_easy_read:
Printing paper: Special printmaking paper can absorb the ink or paint.
It can produce high-quality prints.
pg111_n0028_easy_read: Inking roller, brayer: A rubber roller that spreads ink or paint evenly on the printing plate.
pg111_n0030_easy_read: Palette or inking plate: A flat surface for rolling out and mixing ink or paint.
pg111_n0032_easy_read:
Drawing tools: Tools for making the image on the printing plate, such as:
- pencils
- brushes
- other mark-making tools
pg112_n0003_easy_read: Stencils and masks: Use these to make clear shapes or patterns on the printing plate.
pg112_n0004_easy_read:
Textures and collage materials: You can add different materials to the printing plate to make interesting textures and effects:
- fabric
- leaves
- textured paper
- other objects
pg112_n0008_easy_read: The following tools and equipment are used in monoprinting:
pg112_n0010_easy_read: Printing press: Artists can use a printing press to put even pressure on the plate. This helps move the image from the plate to the paper in a consistent way. A printing press is not always needed for monoprinting.
pg112_n0011_easy_read: Baren: A baren is a hand-held tool. It puts pressure on the plate during hand-printing. It is especially useful for small works.
pg112_n0012_easy_read: Printing registration system: For monoprints with several layers, artists can use a registration system. This helps line up the different layers accurately.
pg112_n0013_easy_read:
Cleaning supplies: Artists use materials such as:
- rags
- sponges
- solvents
These clean the printing plate between prints or create specific effects.
pg112_n0014_easy_read: Protective gloves and apron: These are essential when working with inks, paints, or cleaning solvents.
pg112_n0018_easy_read: The artists must design an interesting item to print.
pg112_n0019_easy_read:
The artist can get ideas for decorative monoprints from:
- natural things with clear textures
- flowers
- twigs
- places where the monoprint will be used
- events where the monoprint will be used
pg112_n0020_easy_read: Once the design is ready, do the following:
pg112_n0022_easy_read: Set up the work area: Put down newspapers or plastic sheets. This protects your work area from paint spills and smudges.
pg112_n0023_easy_read: Surface preparation: First, choose a smooth surface that does not absorb liquid for the printing plate.
pg112_n0024_easy_read:
Common choices are:
- acrylic sheets
- plexiglass
- a well-polished metal surface
pg112_n0025_easy_read: Ink or paint application: Squeeze a small amount of ink or water-based paint onto the palette.
pg112_n0026_easy_read: You can use one colour. You can also use a mix of colours to create unique effects.
pg113_n0004_easy_read: Put a thin, even layer of ink or paint directly on the surface of the plate.
pg113_n0005_easy_read: Do not use too much paint. Too much paint may smudge the print.

You can use these tools to spread the ink evenly across the plate:

Art in Tanzania includes many kinds of art.
They show the country’s rich history and its cultural, social, political, and economic situation.
pg118_n0009_easy_read:
Art production can be simple or complex.

Art trends simply mean "tendencies in art".
People use this term to show the latest changes in art, such as form, subject, style, or other aesthetic features.
pg118_n0019_easy_read: Tanzania, like other countries around the world, has always had these art trends.
pg118_n0021_easy_read: From rock paintings to modern times, the styles of Tanzanian art have changed over time.
pg118_n0022_easy_read:
Rock painting began with ancient rock painters who lived in the Stone Age.
They used painting to show their feelings and memories.
They painted their life experiences, including hunting and gathering.
pg118_n0023_easy_read:
The oldest paintings from the Stone Age are in the Kondoa Irangi rock shelters in central Tanzania.
See figure five point one.
pg118_n0024_easy_read: Similar rock paintings were later found in several rock shelters around Lake Victoria, in the Mara and Mwanza regions.
pg118_n0026_easy_read:
Some main features of prehistoric rock paintings were:
different geometrical patterns
figures of fauna and flora
paintings made on rock surfaces

pg119_n0005_easy_read: The Tingatinga Painting School and the Modern Makonde Sculpture Movement have made Tanzania known around the world for art.
pg119_n0007_easy_read: People can see the influence of Tanzanian paintings and sculptures inside the country and outside the country.
pg119_n0008_easy_read: Tanzanian artists also get ideas and inspiration from other countries or from different regions of Tanzania. These regions develop their own artistic traditions.

pg120_n0006_easy_read: The Tingatinga painting movement first started with a Tanzanian man called Edward Said Tingatinga. He was born in nineteen thirty-two in Mindu village, Tunduru district, Ruvuma region.
pg120_n0007_easy_read: This type of art is named after its founder.
pg120_n0008_easy_read: Edward Said Tingatinga first got ideas for painting in Mindu village. In that village, mural painting in folk art tradition was part of his people's cultural heritage.
pg120_n0009_easy_read: Artists from Zaire, now D R C, also inspired Tingatinga. They used to sell their artworks to foreigners in curio shops in Dar es Salaam.
pg120_n0010_easy_read: This inspiration led him to start painting.
pg120_n0011_easy_read: Tingatinga started painting in Dar es Salaam in nineteen sixty-eight. He found out that painting could bring in some income.
pg120_n0013_easy_read: Tingatinga died tragically because of mistaken identity.
pg120_n0014_easy_read: His taxi driver did not obey a police order to stop. This upset the police patrol. The police patrol started a car chase. The car chase ended in a shootout that killed Edward Said Tingatinga.

pg138_n0038_easy_read: During the colonial period, several talented Africans received formal training. They trained to become professional painters and art teachers. They studied in various schools in Tanzania and at Makerere University College in Uganda.
pg138_n0039_easy_read: Abdullah Farahani, Sam Ntiro, Fatma Abdullah, Professor Elias Jengo, and Raza Mohamed are among the few Tanzanian painters who received formal training in visual art.
pg139_n0004_easy_read: After independence, the production and promotion of formal visual art grew in the country. This included: printmaking; graphics; textiles and fashion design; animation design.
pg139_n0005_easy_read: Western cultural patrons chose trained art scholars. These art scholars became ambassadors of modern art.
pg139_n0007_easy_read: During independence, most of these artists took part in art training programmes. They mainly studied: drawing; painting; printmaking.
pg139_n0008_easy_read: Since nineteen seventy, the Tanzania government has provided art education at Chang’ombe Teachers College and Butimba Teachers College. It also started several art projects at the Nyumba ya Sanaa Art Project and the Tingatinga Arts Society in Dar es Salaam.
pg139_n0009_easy_read: Other developments included the opening of the Bagamoyo College of Art in nineteen eighty. Later, in two thousand and seven, it became Taasisi ya Sanaa na Utamaduni Bagamoyo, TaSUBa. Young talented fine and performing artists studied there.

Occupational health and environmental care are two different fields.
They share one goal.
The goal is to support the social well-being of people in the workplace.
pg143_n0022_easy_read:
Both fields are important for public health.
They help keep people safe and prevent harm from environmental hazards.
pg143_n0023_easy_read:
The goal is to reduce the effect of waste on the environment.
This happens by reducing the amount of waste created by:
- industry
- technology
- our daily activities
pg143_n0027_easy_read: Waste means materials that the producer does not want.
pg143_n0028_easy_read: These materials must be managed to make everyone in that environment safe.
pg144_n0004_easy_read: Waste management is the process of managing waste from when it is made to its final disposal.
pg144_n0008_easy_read: Waste management uses different ways to prevent waste from harming the environment and human health.
pg144_n0009_easy_read: The following points show why waste management is important:
pg144_n0011_easy_read:
Preserving natural resources and reducing pollution:
Good waste management helps protect the environment.
pg144_n0013_easy_read:
Public health:
Waste management removes places where pests can grow.
This helps stop the spread of disease.
pg144_n0015_easy_read:
Sustainability:
If we reduce, reuse, and recycle waste, we can protect the environment.
We can also reduce the amount of waste dumped in landfills.
